questions.stem: The position of a particle moving along the \(x\)-axis is \(x(t)=2t^3-9t^2+12t\), where \(x\) is in meters and \(t\) is in seconds. At what times is the particle momentarily at rest?
questions.explanation: The velocity is \(v=\dfrac{dx}{dt}=6t^2-18t+12=6(t-1)(t-2)\), which is zero at \(t=1\text{ s}\) and \(t=2\text{ s}\). The time \(t=1.5\text{ s}\) is when the acceleration is zero.

questions.stem: The position of a particle moving along the \(x\)-axis is \(x(t)=2t^3-9t^2+12t\), where \(x\) is in meters and \(t\) is in seconds. What total distance does the particle travel between \(t=0\) and \(t=3\text{ s}\)?
questions.explanation: The particle reverses at \(t=1\text{ s}\) and \(t=2\text{ s}\). With \(x(0)=0\), \(x(1)=5\), \(x(2)=4\), and \(x(3)=9\text{ m}\), the distance is \(5+1+5=11\text{ m}\). The displacement is only \(9\text{ m}\).

questions.stem: A particle moves along the \(x\)-axis with acceleration \(a(t)=6t-4\), in \(\text{m/s}^2\). At \(t=0\) its velocity is \(2\text{ m/s}\) and its position is \(x=0\). What is its position at \(t=2\text{ s}\)?
questions.explanation: Integrating, \(v(t)=3t^2-4t+2\) and \(x(t)=t^3-2t^2+2t\). At \(t=2\text{ s}\), \(x=8-8+4=4\text{ m}\). Omitting the initial velocity gives \(0\).

questions.skill: Velocity as a function of position
questions.stem: The velocity of a particle moving along the \(x\)-axis depends on its position according to \(v=kx\), where \(k\) is a positive constant. What is the particle's acceleration as a function of \(x\)?
questions.explanation: By the chain rule, \(a=\dfrac{dv}{dt}=\dfrac{dv}{dx}\dfrac{dx}{dt}=v\dfrac{dv}{dx}=(kx)(k)=k^2x\). The derivative \(\dfrac{dv}{dx}=k\) alone is not the acceleration.

questions.stem: A particle starts from rest at \(t=0\) and moves along a line with the acceleration shown in the graph. At what time is its speed greatest during the interval \(0\le t\le 6\text{ s}\)?
choices: At every time from \(t=0\) to \(t=2\text{ s}\)
questions.explanation: The velocity keeps increasing as long as the acceleration is positive, which is until the graph crosses zero at \(t=4\text{ s}\). After that the acceleration is negative and the velocity, still positive, decreases. The acceleration is greatest before \(2\text{ s}\), but the velocity is not.

questions.stem: A particle starts from rest at \(t=0\) and moves along a line with the acceleration shown in the graph. What is its velocity at \(t=6\text{ s}\)?
questions.explanation: The change in velocity is the signed area under the graph: \(8+4=12\text{ m/s}\) from \(0\) to \(4\text{ s}\), then \(-4\text{ m/s}\) from \(4\) to \(6\text{ s}\), for a total of \(8\text{ m/s}\).

questions.stem: The position of a projectile is \(\vec r(t)=(3t)\,\hat\imath+(4t-5t^2)\,\hat\jmath\), in meters, with \(t\) in seconds. What is the speed of the projectile at \(t=0.8\text{ s}\)?
questions.explanation: The velocity is \(\vec v=3\,\hat\imath+(4-10t)\,\hat\jmath\). At \(t=0.8\text{ s}\) this is \(3\,\hat\imath-4\,\hat\jmath\), with magnitude \(5\text{ m/s}\). The projectile has returned to its launch height and has its launch speed.

questions.stem: A particle starts from rest and has acceleration \(\vec a(t)=2\,\hat\imath-4t\,\hat\jmath\), in \(\text{m/s}^2\). What is its speed at \(t=1\text{ s}\)?
questions.explanation: Integrating each component from rest gives \(\vec v=2t\,\hat\imath-2t^2\,\hat\jmath\). At \(t=1\text{ s}\), \(\vec v=2\,\hat\imath-2\,\hat\jmath\), with magnitude \(2\sqrt{2}\text{ m/s}\). The value \(2\sqrt{5}\) is the magnitude of the acceleration at that time.

questions.stem: A car travels around a curve at constant speed. Which statement about its acceleration is correct?
choices: It is zero, because the speed is constant.
It is parallel to the velocity, because the car is moving forward.
It is directed away from the center of the curve.
It is perpendicular to the velocity and directed toward the inside of the curve.
questions.explanation: Acceleration is the rate of change of the velocity vector. At constant speed only the direction of the velocity changes, so the acceleration has no component along the velocity; it points toward the center of curvature.

questions.stem: Two projectiles are launched from level ground with the same speed, one at \(30^\circ\) and one at \(60^\circ\) above the horizontal. Air resistance is negligible. What is the ratio of the time of flight of the \(60^\circ\) projectile to that of the \(30^\circ\) projectile?
questions.explanation: The time of flight is \(\dfrac{2v_0\sin\theta}{g}\), so the ratio is \(\dfrac{\sin 60^\circ}{\sin 30^\circ}=\sqrt{3}\). The two projectiles have the same range, but not the same time of flight.

questions.stem: A boat's engine is shut off when the boat is moving at speed \(v_0\). Afterward its velocity is \(v(t)=v_0e^{-kt}\), where \(k\) is a positive constant. How far does the boat travel after the engine is shut off?
choices: It travels an unlimited distance, because it never stops.
questions.explanation: The distance is \(\displaystyle\int_0^\infty v_0e^{-kt}\,dt=\dfrac{v_0}{k}\). Although the velocity never reaches exactly zero, the total distance is finite because the integral converges.

questions.stem: The graph shows the positions of carts A and B as functions of time. The curve for cart B is a parabola. What is the acceleration of cart B?
questions.explanation: Cart B starts from rest at the origin and is at \(x=8\text{ m}\) at \(t=4\text{ s}\). With \(x=\tfrac{1}{2}at^2\), \(8=\tfrac{1}{2}a(16)\), so \(a=1\text{ m/s}^2\). The value \(2\text{ m/s}\) is the constant speed of cart A.

questions.stem: A particle's position is \(\vec r(t)=R\cos(\omega t)\,\hat\imath+R\sin(\omega t)\,\hat\jmath\), where \(R\) and \(\omega\) are constants. Which expression gives its acceleration?
questions.explanation: Differentiating twice gives \(\vec a=-\omega^2R\cos(\omega t)\,\hat\imath-\omega^2R\sin(\omega t)\,\hat\jmath=-\omega^2\vec r\). The acceleration has magnitude \(\omega^2R\) and points toward the center of the circle.

questions.stem: A car starts from rest and travels around a circular track of radius \(R\) with speed \(v=bt\), where \(b\) is a constant. What is the magnitude of the car's acceleration at time \(t\)?
questions.explanation: The tangential component is \(\dfrac{dv}{dt}=b\) and the centripetal component is \(\dfrac{v^2}{R}=\dfrac{b^2t^2}{R}\). They are perpendicular, so the magnitude is the square root of the sum of their squares, not their sum.

questions.stem: An object moves along a line with constant, nonzero acceleration from time \(t_1\) to time \(t_2\). At which instant does its instantaneous velocity equal its average velocity for the interval?
choices: At the instant it reaches the midpoint of the distance traveled
At no instant, because the velocity is always changing
At the midpoint of the interval in time, \(\dfrac{t_1+t_2}{2}\)
questions.explanation: With constant acceleration the velocity changes linearly in time, so its average over the interval is \(\dfrac{v_1+v_2}{2}\), which is the value it has halfway through the interval in time. The object reaches the spatial midpoint at a different instant.

questions.stem: A particle moves along a line with the velocity \(v(t)=6t-3t^2\), in meters per second, shown in the graph. What is its displacement from \(t=0\) to \(t=3\text{ s}\)?
questions.explanation: The displacement is \(\displaystyle\int_0^3\left(6t-3t^2\right)dt=\left[3t^2-t^3\right]_0^3=27-27=0\). The particle travels forward and then returns to its starting point. The value \(-9\text{ m/s}\) is the velocity at \(t=3\text{ s}\), not a displacement.

questions.stem: A particle moves along a line with the velocity \(v(t)=6t-3t^2\), in meters per second, shown in the graph. What total distance does it travel from \(t=0\) to \(t=3\text{ s}\)?
questions.explanation: The velocity changes sign at \(t=2\text{ s}\). From \(0\) to \(2\text{ s}\) the particle moves \(\left[3t^2-t^3\right]_0^2=4\text{ m}\) forward, and from \(2\) to \(3\text{ s}\) it moves \(\left|0-4\right|=4\text{ m}\) back. The distance is the integral of the speed, \(8\text{ m}\).

questions.stem: A particle moves along a line with the velocity \(v(t)=6t-3t^2\), in meters per second, shown in the graph. What is its acceleration at \(t=2\text{ s}\), the instant its velocity is zero?
questions.explanation: \(a=\dfrac{dv}{dt}=6-6t\), which is \(-6\text{ m/s}^2\) at \(t=2\text{ s}\). A particle can be momentarily at rest while accelerating; that is how it reverses direction.

questions.stem: A particle moves along a line with the velocity \(v(t)=6t-3t^2\) shown in the graph. During which time intervals is the particle's speed increasing?
questions.explanation: Speed increases when velocity and acceleration have the same sign. With \(a=6-6t\): both are positive for \(0<t<1\text{ s}\), the signs differ for \(1<t<2\text{ s}\), and both are negative for \(2<t<3\text{ s}\), when the particle speeds up moving backward.

questions.skill: Acceleration from velocity as a function of position
questions.stem: A particle's velocity depends on its position according to \(v=3\sqrt{x}\), with \(v\) in meters per second and \(x\) in meters. What is the particle's acceleration?
questions.explanation: \(a=v\dfrac{dv}{dx}=3\sqrt{x}\cdot\dfrac{3}{2\sqrt{x}}=4.5\text{ m/s}^2\). Equivalently, \(v^2=9x\) has the form \(v^2=2ax\) for constant acceleration from rest. The expression \(\dfrac{dv}{dx}\) alone is not the acceleration.

questions.stem: A ball is thrown horizontally at \(10\text{ m/s}\) from the top of a long slope inclined at \(45^\circ\) below the horizontal. Using \(g=10\text{ m/s}^2\) and neglecting air resistance, how long after it is thrown does the ball land on the slope?
questions.explanation: The ball lands where its vertical drop equals its horizontal distance, because \(\tan 45^\circ=1\): \(\tfrac{1}{2}gt^2=v_0t\), so \(t=\dfrac{2v_0}{g}=2.0\text{ s}\).

questions.stem: Rain falls vertically at \(8.0\text{ m/s}\) relative to the ground. A car drives horizontally at \(6.0\text{ m/s}\). What is the speed of the rain relative to the car?
questions.explanation: The rain's velocity relative to the car is \(\vec v_{\text{rain}}-\vec v_{\text{car}}\), which has components \(6.0\text{ m/s}\) backward and \(8.0\text{ m/s}\) downward. Its magnitude is \(\sqrt{6.0^2+8.0^2}=10\text{ m/s}\), so the rain appears to slant toward the car's windshield.

questions.stem: A particle moves along a line with velocity \(v(t)=4-2t\), in meters per second. What is its average speed from \(t=0\) to \(t=4\text{ s}\)?
questions.explanation: The velocity changes sign at \(t=2\text{ s}\). The particle moves \(4\text{ m}\) forward and then \(4\text{ m}\) back, so the distance is \(8\text{ m}\) and the average speed is \(\dfrac{8}{4}=2\text{ m/s}\). The average velocity is zero because the displacement is zero.

questions.stem: A projectile is launched from level ground at \(45^\circ\) above the horizontal. Air resistance is negligible. What is the ratio of its maximum height to its horizontal range?
questions.explanation: The maximum height is \(\dfrac{v_0^2\sin^2 45^\circ}{2g}=\dfrac{v_0^2}{4g}\) and the range is \(\dfrac{v_0^2\sin 90^\circ}{g}=\dfrac{v_0^2}{g}\). Their ratio is \(\dfrac{1}{4}\) for every launch speed.

questions.stem: The graph of a particle's position as a function of time is a parabola opening upward with its vertex at \(t=2\text{ s}\). Which describes the graph of its velocity as a function of time?
choices: A straight line with negative slope that crosses zero at \(t=2\text{ s}\)
A horizontal line, because the acceleration is constant
A straight line with positive slope that crosses zero at \(t=2\text{ s}\)
A parabola with its vertex at \(t=2\text{ s}\)
questions.explanation: The derivative of a quadratic is linear. The position graph has zero slope at its vertex, so the velocity is zero at \(t=2\text{ s}\), and a parabola opening upward has an increasing slope, so the velocity line rises.

questions.stem: A particle moves so that its velocity is perpendicular to its acceleration at every instant. Which of the following must be true?
choices: It moves in a straight line.
questions.explanation: \(\dfrac{d}{dt}\left(\vec v\cdot\vec v\right)=2\,\vec v\cdot\vec a=0\), so the square of the speed does not change. The direction of motion can change, as in uniform circular motion, so the velocity need not be constant.

questions.stem: For which kind of motion along a line is the average velocity over any time interval always equal to the mean of the initial and final velocities?
choices: Any motion in which the velocity is always positive
Motion with an acceleration that increases linearly with time
Motion in which the object starts from rest
questions.explanation: With constant acceleration, velocity is a linear function of time, and the average of a linear function over an interval equals the average of its end values. For a curved velocity graph, the area under it generally differs from that of the trapezoid through its endpoints.

questions.stem: Two projectiles are launched from level ground with the same speed, one at \(30^\circ\) and one at \(60^\circ\) above the horizontal. Air resistance is negligible. How do their ranges and maximum heights compare?
choices: Their ranges and maximum heights are both equal.
Their ranges are equal, and the \(60^\circ\) projectile rises three times as high.
The \(60^\circ\) projectile has the greater range and rises three times as high.
The \(30^\circ\) projectile has the greater range, and their heights are equal.
questions.explanation: The range is proportional to \(\sin 2\theta\), which is the same for \(30^\circ\) and \(60^\circ\). The maximum height is proportional to \(\sin^2\theta\): \(\tfrac{3}{4}\) versus \(\tfrac{1}{4}\), a ratio of 3.

questions.stem: A ball is thrown straight up and air resistance is not negligible. What is the magnitude of the ball's acceleration at the instant it reaches its highest point?
choices: Greater than \(g\), because drag still acts downward at the top
Exactly \(g\), because the ball is momentarily at rest and experiences no drag
Less than \(g\), because drag acts upward at the top
Zero, because the ball is momentarily at rest
questions.explanation: Drag depends on the velocity relative to the air, and at the top the velocity is zero, so only gravity acts. On the way up the acceleration is greater than \(g\), and on the way down it is less.

questions.stem: An object of mass \(m\) is released from rest and falls subject to gravity and a drag force of magnitude \(bv\). Which expression gives its speed as a function of time?
questions.explanation: Newton's second law gives \(m\dfrac{dv}{dt}=mg-bv\). Separating variables and integrating from rest gives \(v=\dfrac{mg}{b}\left(1-e^{-bt/m}\right)\), which starts at zero and approaches the terminal speed \(\dfrac{mg}{b}\). The exponent must be dimensionless, which rules out \(e^{-mt/b}\).

figure.alt: Speed versus time graph for an object falling from rest with air resistance: the speed rises quickly at first and levels off, approaching a dashed horizontal line at 20 meters per second

questions.stem: The graph shows the speed of an object falling from rest subject to gravity and a drag force proportional to its speed. What is the magnitude of the object's acceleration at the instant its speed is \(10\text{ m/s}\)?
questions.explanation: The terminal speed is \(20\text{ m/s}\), where the drag force equals the weight. Because drag is proportional to speed, at \(10\text{ m/s}\) it is half the weight, so the net force is \(\tfrac{1}{2}mg\) and the acceleration is \(\tfrac{1}{2}g\).

questions.stem: A skydiver of mass \(m\) experiences a drag force of magnitude \(cv^2\) and reaches terminal speed \(v_T\). A second skydiver with the same shape and drag coefficient \(c\) has mass \(4m\). What is the second skydiver's terminal speed?
questions.explanation: At terminal speed \(cv^2=mg\), so \(v_T=\sqrt{\dfrac{mg}{c}}\). Quadrupling the mass doubles the terminal speed.

questions.stem: An object of mass \(m\) falls from rest subject to gravity and a drag force of magnitude \(bv\). At time \(t=\dfrac{m}{b}\), what fraction of its terminal speed has it reached?
questions.explanation: The speed is \(v_T\left(1-e^{-bt/m}\right)\). At \(t=\dfrac{m}{b}\) the exponent is \(-1\), so \(v=v_T\left(1-e^{-1}\right)\approx 0.63\,v_T\). The quantity \(\dfrac{m}{b}\) is the time constant of the motion.

questions.stem: A \(2\text{ kg}\) object at rest at the origin is acted on by a net force \(F(t)=6t\), in newtons, along the \(x\)-axis. What is its position at \(t=2\text{ s}\)?
questions.explanation: The acceleration is \(a=3t\), so \(v=\tfrac{3}{2}t^2\) and \(x=\tfrac{1}{2}t^3\). At \(t=2\text{ s}\), \(x=4\text{ m}\). The velocity at that time is \(6\text{ m/s}\).

questions.stem: A car rounds a banked curve of radius \(r\) at speed \(v\). At what banking angle \(\theta\), measured from the horizontal, can the car make the turn with no friction force from the road?
questions.explanation: With no friction, the vertical component of the normal force balances gravity, \(N\cos\theta=mg\), and its horizontal component supplies the centripetal force, \(N\sin\theta=\dfrac{mv^2}{r}\). Dividing gives \(\tan\theta=\dfrac{v^2}{rg}\).

questions.stem: A ball on a string of length \(L\) moves in a horizontal circle, with the string making a constant angle \(\theta\) with the vertical, as shown. What is the period of the motion?
questions.explanation: Vertically, \(T\cos\theta=mg\). Horizontally, \(T\sin\theta=m\omega^2(L\sin\theta)\), so \(T=m\omega^2L\). Combining, \(\omega^2=\dfrac{g}{L\cos\theta}\), and the period is \(\dfrac{2\pi}{\omega}\).

questions.stem: A moon orbits a planet in a circular orbit of radius \(r\) with period \(T\). A second moon orbits the same planet in a circular orbit with period \(8T\). What is the radius of the second moon's orbit?
questions.explanation: For circular orbits around the same body, \(T^2\propto r^3\). Multiplying the period by 8 multiplies \(T^2\) by 64, so \(r^3\) increases by a factor of 64 and \(r\) by a factor of 4.

questions.stem: A block rests on a frictionless wedge inclined at angle \(\theta\), as shown. The wedge is pushed horizontally so that the block does not slide along the incline. What is the magnitude of the wedge's acceleration?
questions.explanation: The only forces on the block are gravity and the normal force. Vertically, \(N\cos\theta=mg\); horizontally, \(N\sin\theta=ma\). Dividing gives \(a=g\tan\theta\). The value \(g\sin\theta\) is the acceleration down the incline when the wedge is at rest.

questions.stem: A uniform rope of mass \(M\) and length \(L\) hangs vertically from a ceiling. What is the tension in the rope at a point a distance \(y\) above its lower end?
questions.explanation: Each point of the rope supports the weight of the rope below it. The portion below has mass \(\dfrac{My}{L}\), so the tension is \(\dfrac{Mgy}{L}\), increasing from zero at the bottom to \(Mg\) at the ceiling.

questions.stem: Block \(m_1\) slides on a table with coefficient of kinetic friction \(\mu_k\) and is connected by a light string over a light, frictionless pulley to hanging block \(m_2\), which is descending, as shown. What is the magnitude of the acceleration of the blocks?
questions.explanation: Treating the two blocks as one system, the net force along the direction of motion is \(m_2g-\mu_km_1g\) and the total mass is \(m_1+m_2\). The friction force acts only on \(m_1\), but both blocks must be accelerated.

questions.stem: A ball on a string of length \(R\) moves in a vertical circle, as shown. What is the minimum speed the ball must have at the bottom of the circle in order to complete the circle with the string taut?
questions.explanation: At the top the string just stays taut when gravity alone provides the centripetal force, so \(v_{\text{top}}^2=gR\). Energy conservation gives \(v_{\text{bottom}}^2=v_{\text{top}}^2+4gR=5gR\). A speed of \(2\sqrt{gR}\) would bring the ball to the top with zero speed, which a string cannot support.

questions.stem: A puck of mass \(m\) slides on a horizontal surface with initial speed \(v_0\). The only horizontal force on it is a drag force of magnitude \(bv\). How far does the puck travel before coming to rest?
questions.explanation: From \(m\dfrac{dv}{dt}=-bv\) and \(\dfrac{dv}{dt}=v\dfrac{dv}{dx}\), \(m\,dv=-b\,dx\). Integrating from \(v_0\) to \(0\) gives \(x=\dfrac{mv_0}{b}\). Equivalently, \(v=v_0e^{-bt/m}\) integrates to the same distance.

questions.stem: An object of mass \(m\) falls vertically subject to gravity and a drag force whose magnitude is proportional to the square of its speed, with constant of proportionality \(c\). Taking downward as positive, which differential equation describes its motion?
questions.explanation: With downward positive, gravity contributes \(+mg\) and drag, which opposes the downward motion, contributes \(-cv^2\). Setting \(\dfrac{dv}{dt}=0\) gives the terminal speed \(\sqrt{\dfrac{mg}{c}}\).

questions.stem: A planet of radius \(R\) has uniform density, and the gravitational field strength at its surface is \(g_s\). What is the gravitational field strength at a distance \(\dfrac{R}{2}\) from the planet's center?
questions.explanation: Only the mass inside radius \(r\) contributes to the field there, and that mass is proportional to \(r^3\). The field is \(\dfrac{GM_{\text{enc}}}{r^2}\propto r\), so at half the radius it is half the surface value. The inverse-square result \(4g_s\) applies only outside the planet.

questions.stem: A \(2.0\text{ kg}\) block rests on a \(4.0\text{ kg}\) block, which sits on a frictionless floor, as shown. The coefficient of static friction between the blocks is 0.50. What is the greatest horizontal force \(F\) that can be applied to the top block without it slipping on the bottom block? Use \(g=10\text{ m/s}^2\).
questions.explanation: Friction from the top block is the only horizontal force on the bottom block, and it can be at most \(0.50(2.0)(10)=10\text{ N}\), giving the bottom block at most \(2.5\text{ m/s}^2\). Both blocks share that acceleration, so \(F=(6.0)(2.5)=15\text{ N}\). The value \(10\text{ N}\) is the friction limit, not the applied force.

questions.stem: A puck of mass \(m\) slides on a horizontal surface, and the only horizontal force on it is a drag force of magnitude \(bv\). How long does its speed take to fall to half its initial value?
questions.explanation: \(m\dfrac{dv}{dt}=-bv\) gives \(v=v_0e^{-bt/m}\). Setting \(e^{-bt/m}=\tfrac{1}{2}\) gives \(t=\dfrac{m}{b}\ln 2\). The speed never actually reaches zero.

questions.stem: An object falls with a drag force proportional to the square of its speed and has terminal speed \(v_T\). What is the magnitude of its acceleration when its speed is \(\tfrac{1}{2}v_T\)?
questions.explanation: At terminal speed \(cv_T^2=mg\), so the acceleration is \(g-\dfrac{cv^2}{m}=g\left(1-\dfrac{v^2}{v_T^2}\right)\). At half the terminal speed the drag is one fourth of the weight, so \(a=\tfrac{3}{4}g\). Linear drag would give \(\tfrac{1}{2}g\).

questions.stem: A coin rests on a horizontal turntable a distance \(r\) from the axis. The coefficient of static friction is \(\mu_s\). What is the greatest angular speed at which the turntable can rotate without the coin sliding?
questions.explanation: Static friction supplies the centripetal force, so \(m\omega^2r\le\mu_smg\), giving \(\omega\le\sqrt{\dfrac{\mu_sg}{r}}\). The expression \(\sqrt{\mu_sgr}\) is the maximum linear speed.

questions.stem: A small ball of mass \(m\) is whirled in a horizontal circle on a frictionless table at angular speed \(\omega\), attached to a uniform string of mass \(M\) and length \(L\) whose other end is fixed at the center. What is the tension in the string at the center?
questions.explanation: The tension at the center must supply the centripetal force for everything outside it. The ball needs \(m\omega^2L\), and the string needs \(\displaystyle\int_0^L\dfrac{M}{L}\omega^2r\,dr=\tfrac{1}{2}M\omega^2L\), since its mass is spread out at an average radius of \(\dfrac{L}{2}\).

questions.stem: A curve of radius \(r\) is banked at angle \(\theta\), and the coefficient of static friction between the tires and road is \(\mu\). What is the greatest speed at which a car can round the curve without sliding up the bank?
questions.explanation: At the greatest speed, static friction acts down the bank with magnitude \(\mu N\). Vertically, \(N\cos\theta-\mu N\sin\theta=mg\); horizontally, \(N\sin\theta+\mu N\cos\theta=\dfrac{mv^2}{r}\). Dividing eliminates \(N\). The second expression is the least speed, when friction acts up the bank.

questions.stem: A planet of radius \(R\) has a gravitational field strength \(g\) at its surface. How short would its rotation period have to be for objects at its equator to have zero apparent weight?
questions.explanation: An object at the equator has zero apparent weight when gravity alone provides exactly the centripetal force, \(mg=m\omega^2R\). Then \(\omega=\sqrt{\dfrac{g}{R}}\), and the period is \(\dfrac{2\pi}{\omega}\). For Earth this is about 84 minutes.

questions.stem: A block of mass \(m\) rests on a floor with coefficients of static and kinetic friction \(\mu_s\) and \(\mu_k\). A horizontal force \(F=kt\), where \(k\) is a constant, is applied starting at \(t=0\). At what time does the block begin to move?
questions.explanation: Static friction matches the applied force until the force reaches its maximum value \(\mu_smg\). Setting \(kt=\mu_smg\) gives the time. After the block starts moving, the smaller kinetic friction acts, so the block jumps to a nonzero acceleration.

questions.stem: A ball on a string moves in a horizontal circle as a conical pendulum, as shown. How does the tension in the string compare with the ball's weight?
choices: It equals the weight, because the ball does not move vertically.
It is always greater than the weight.
It is less than the weight, because the string is tilted.
It can be greater or less than the weight, depending on the speed.
questions.explanation: The vertical component of the tension balances gravity, \(T\cos\theta=mg\), so \(T=\dfrac{mg}{\cos\theta}>mg\) for any tilt. The horizontal component supplies the centripetal force.

questions.stem: A horse pulls a cart forward and both speed up together. A student argues that the cart pulls back on the horse with an equal force, so the two cannot accelerate. Which statement correctly resolves the argument?
choices: The horse's pull on the cart is actually larger than the cart's pull on the horse.
Newton's third law applies only to objects at rest.
The forces cancel, and the motion is caused by the cart's inertia.
The two equal forces act on different objects; the cart accelerates because the horse's pull exceeds the other forces on the cart.
questions.explanation: A third-law pair never acts on the same object, so the pair cannot cancel. Each object's acceleration depends on the net force on that object: the cart's on the horse's pull and friction, the horse's on the ground's push and the cart's pull.

questions.stem: Two balls with the same size and shape fall from rest through air with a drag force \(bv\), where \(b\) is the same for both. Ball 1 has twice the mass of ball 2. Which reaches the ground first?
choices: Ball 1, because its terminal speed is twice as great
Ball 2, because it experiences less drag
They arrive together, because gravity gives both the same acceleration
Ball 2, because a smaller mass accelerates more easily
questions.explanation: The acceleration is \(g-\dfrac{b}{m}v\), so at any speed drag slows the heavier ball less. Its terminal speed \(\dfrac{mg}{b}\) is twice as large, so it is faster at every moment after release.

questions.skill: Apparent weight on a rotating planet
questions.stem: Ignoring Earth's slightly flattened shape, why does a person standing on a scale at the equator read slightly less than the same person standing at a pole?
choices: The gravitational force is weaker at the equator because Earth is spinning.
Air pressure pushes upward more strongly at the equator.
At the equator part of the gravitational force must provide the centripetal acceleration of Earth's rotation, so the normal force is smaller.
The scale reads more at the poles because the person is closer to Earth's axis.
questions.explanation: At the equator the person moves in a circle, so \(mg-N=m\omega^2R\), and the scale reads \(N\). At a pole the person is on the axis and does not move in a circle, so \(N=mg\).

questions.stem: A thin, uniform spherical shell of mass \(M\) is far from any other object. What is the gravitational field at a point inside the shell, away from its center?
choices: Directed toward the center, with magnitude \(\dfrac{GM}{r^2}\)
Directed toward the nearest part of the shell
Directed away from the center, with magnitude \(\dfrac{GM}{R^2}\)
questions.explanation: The pulls from opposite parts of the shell cancel exactly: a nearer patch is closer but contains proportionally less mass, by the inverse-square law. This result is why only the mass inside radius \(r\) matters inside a planet.

questions.stem: An object is dropped from rest and falls with a drag force proportional to its speed. Which describes a graph of its acceleration as a function of time?
choices: It decreases linearly from \(g\) to zero and stays at zero.
It decreases exponentially from \(g\) toward zero.
questions.explanation: The velocity is \(v_T\left(1-e^{-bt/m}\right)\), so its derivative is \(a=ge^{-bt/m}\). The acceleration starts at \(g\), when the speed and drag are zero, and approaches zero as the speed approaches the terminal speed.

questions.stem: A particle moves along the \(x\)-axis from \(x=0\) to \(x=2\text{ m}\) under a force \(F(x)=3x^2-2x\), in newtons. How much work does the force do on the particle?
questions.explanation: \(W=\displaystyle\int_0^2\left(3x^2-2x\right)dx=\left[x^3-x^2\right]_0^2=8-4=4\text{ J}\). Multiplying the force at \(x=2\text{ m}\), which is \(8\text{ N}\), by a distance is not valid for a force that varies.

figure.alt: Potential energy versus position graph. The curve starts at 0 joules at x = 0, rises to a local maximum of 4 joules at x = 1 meter, falls to a local minimum of 0 joules at x = 3 meters, and rises again, reaching 4 joules at x = 4 meters

questions.stem: The graph shows the potential energy \(U(x)=x^3-6x^2+9x\), in joules, of a system as a function of the position \(x\), in meters, of a particle. At which position is the particle in stable equilibrium?
questions.explanation: Equilibrium occurs where \(F=-\dfrac{dU}{dx}=0\), at \(x=1\text{ m}\) and \(x=3\text{ m}\). At the minimum, \(x=3\text{ m}\), a small displacement produces a force back toward equilibrium, so it is stable. The maximum at \(x=1\text{ m}\) is an unstable equilibrium.

figure.alt: Potential energy versus position graph. The curve starts at 0 joules at x = 0, rises to a local maximum of 4 joules at x = 1 meter, falls to a local minimum of 0 joules at x = 3 meters, and rises again, reaching 4 joules at x = 4 meters

questions.stem: The graph shows the potential energy \(U(x)=x^3-6x^2+9x\), in joules, of a system as a function of the position \(x\), in meters, of a particle. What force acts on the particle at \(x=2\text{ m}\)?
questions.explanation: \(F=-\dfrac{dU}{dx}=-\left(3x^2-12x+9\right)\). At \(x=2\text{ m}\), \(F=-(12-24+9)=+3\text{ N}\). The potential energy decreases toward larger \(x\) there, so the force points in the \(+x\) direction.

questions.stem: The graph shows the potential energy \(U(x)=x^3-6x^2+9x\), in joules, of a system as a function of the position \(x\), in meters, of a particle. The particle is released from rest at \(x=2\text{ m}\), and no other forces do work. Between which positions does it move?
choices: From \(x=2\text{ m}\) toward \(x=0\), where the potential energy is zero
questions.explanation: The total energy is \(U(2)=2\text{ J}\). The force at \(x=2\text{ m}\) is in the \(+x\) direction, so the particle moves through the minimum and stops where \(U\) again equals \(2\text{ J}\). Solving \(x^3-6x^2+9x=2\) gives \((x-2)(x^2-4x+1)=0\), so the far turning point is \(x=2+\sqrt{3}\approx 3.7\text{ m}\).

questions.stem: A force \(\vec F=2\,\hat\imath+3\,\hat\jmath\), in newtons, acts on a particle moving with velocity \(\vec v=4\,\hat\imath-\hat\jmath\), in meters per second. What is the instantaneous power delivered by the force?
questions.explanation: Power is the dot product \(\vec F\cdot\vec v=(2)(4)+(3)(-1)=5\text{ W}\). Multiplying the magnitudes ignores the angle between the vectors.

questions.stem: An engine delivers constant power \(P\) to a car of mass \(m\) that starts from rest on a level road. Resistive forces are negligible. Which expression gives the distance the car has traveled at time \(t\)?
questions.explanation: The work done, \(Pt\), equals the kinetic energy, so \(v=\sqrt{\dfrac{2Pt}{m}}\). Integrating, \(x=\sqrt{\dfrac{2P}{m}}\cdot\dfrac{2}{3}t^{3/2}\). The acceleration is not constant, so \(x\) is not proportional to \(t^2\).

questions.skill: Potential energy of a nonlinear spring
questions.stem: A spring exerts a restoring force \(F(x)=-kx-\beta x^3\) when stretched a distance \(x\) from equilibrium, where \(k\) and \(\beta\) are positive constants. Taking \(U=0\) at \(x=0\), what is the potential energy stored in the spring?
questions.explanation: \(U(x)=-\displaystyle\int_0^xF\,dx'=\int_0^x\left(kx'+\beta x'^3\right)dx'=\tfrac{1}{2}kx^2+\tfrac{1}{4}\beta x^4\). The potential energy is positive because work must be done against the restoring force.

questions.stem: A projectile is launched straight up from the surface of a planet of radius \(R\) with half the planet's escape speed. The planet has no atmosphere and does not rotate. What maximum height above the surface does the projectile reach?
questions.explanation: The escape speed satisfies \(v_e^2=\dfrac{2GM}{R}\), so the launch speed has \(v^2=\dfrac{GM}{2R}\). Energy conservation, \(\tfrac{1}{2}v^2-\dfrac{GM}{R}=-\dfrac{GM}{r}\), gives \(\dfrac{GM}{r}=\dfrac{3GM}{4R}\), so \(r=\dfrac{4R}{3}\) and the height is \(\dfrac{R}{3}\). Using \(mgh\) with constant \(g\) gives \(\dfrac{R}{4}\).

questions.stem: A satellite of mass \(m\) is in a circular orbit of radius \(r\) around a planet of mass \(M\). How much energy must be added to move it to a circular orbit of radius \(2r\)?
questions.explanation: In a circular orbit the total mechanical energy is \(E=-\dfrac{GMm}{2r}\). The change is \(-\dfrac{GMm}{4r}-\left(-\dfrac{GMm}{2r}\right)=\dfrac{GMm}{4r}\). The potential energy rises by \(\dfrac{GMm}{2r}\), but the kinetic energy falls by half that amount.

questions.stem: Which of the following is a property of every conservative force?
choices: It does no work on an object that moves along a straight line.
It always acts opposite to the object's velocity.
The work it does on an object that moves around any closed path is zero.
Its magnitude is the same at every position.
questions.explanation: The work done by a conservative force depends only on the starting and ending positions, so it is zero around any closed path and a potential energy function can be defined. Kinetic friction fails this test, because it does negative work over every part of a round trip.

questions.stem: A small block is given a slight push from rest at the top of the fixed, frictionless hemisphere shown. At what height above the ground does the block lose contact with the hemisphere?
questions.explanation: At angle \(\theta\) from the vertical, energy conservation gives \(v^2=2gR(1-\cos\theta)\). Contact is lost when the normal force is zero: \(mg\cos\theta=\dfrac{mv^2}{R}\). Then \(\cos\theta=2(1-\cos\theta)\), so \(\cos\theta=\dfrac{2}{3}\) and the height is \(R\cos\theta=\dfrac{2}{3}R\).

questions.skill: Work by a variable friction force
questions.stem: A block moving with speed \(v_0\) enters a rough horizontal region where the coefficient of kinetic friction increases with the distance \(x\) traveled into the region according to \(\mu_k=bx\), where \(b\) is a constant. How far into the region does the block slide before stopping?
questions.explanation: The friction force is \(bxmg\), so the work it does over a distance \(d\) is \(-\displaystyle\int_0^dbmgx\,dx=-\tfrac{1}{2}bmgd^2\). Setting its magnitude equal to \(\tfrac{1}{2}mv_0^2\) gives \(d=\dfrac{v_0}{\sqrt{bg}}\).

questions.stem: At its top speed on a level road, a car's engine power is used entirely to overcome a drag force proportional to the square of the car's speed. By what factor must the engine power increase to double the top speed?
questions.explanation: At constant speed the driving force equals the drag force, so \(P=Fv\propto v^2\cdot v=v^3\). Doubling the speed requires \(2^3=8\) times the power.

questions.stem: The graph shows the net force \(F=4x-x^2\), in newtons, on an object as a function of its position \(x\), in meters. How much work does the force do as the object moves from \(x=0\) to \(x=4\text{ m}\)?
questions.explanation: \(W=\displaystyle\int_0^4\left(4x-x^2\right)dx=\left[2x^2-\dfrac{x^3}{3}\right]_0^4=32-\dfrac{64}{3}=\dfrac{32}{3}\text{ J}\). Multiplying the peak force by the distance overestimates the work, because the force is less than \(4\text{ N}\) almost everywhere.

questions.stem: A \(2.0\text{ kg}\) object is at rest at \(x=0\) and is acted on by the net force shown in the graph, \(F=4x-x^2\) in newtons. What is its speed at \(x=4\text{ m}\)?
questions.explanation: The net work is \(\dfrac{32}{3}\text{ J}\), which equals the kinetic energy: \(\tfrac{1}{2}(2.0)v^2=\dfrac{32}{3}\), so \(v\approx 3.3\text{ m/s}\). Forgetting the factor of one half gives \(2.3\text{ m/s}\).

questions.stem: The graph shows the potential energy of two atoms as a function of their separation. What is the least energy that must be added to separate the atoms completely, starting from rest at their equilibrium separation?
questions.explanation: At rest at equilibrium the system has \(U=-4\text{ eV}\). Completely separated atoms have \(U\to 0\), so at least \(4\text{ eV}\) must be added. This is the dissociation energy of the molecule.

questions.stem: The graph shows the potential energy of two atoms as a function of their separation \(r\). What is the force between the atoms when \(r=0.9\times 10^{-10}\text{ m}\)?
choices: Repulsive, because \(U\) decreases as \(r\) increases there
Zero, because \(U\) is close to zero there
Attractive, because the atoms are closer than their equilibrium separation
questions.explanation: The force is \(F=-\dfrac{dU}{dr}\). To the left of the minimum the slope is negative, so \(F\) is positive, pushing the atoms apart. The sign of \(U\) itself does not determine the direction of the force; its slope does.

questions.stem: The two atoms whose potential energy is graphed have a total energy of \(-2\text{ eV}\), shown by the dashed line. Which statement describes their motion?
choices: The atoms separate completely, because their kinetic energy is positive.
The separation oscillates between about \(0.92\) and \(1.23\times 10^{-10}\text{ m}\), and the atoms cannot separate.
The separation stays fixed at \(1.0\times 10^{-10}\text{ m}\).
The separation can take any value greater than \(0.92\times 10^{-10}\text{ m}\).
questions.explanation: Kinetic energy is \(E-U\), which cannot be negative, so the atoms are confined to the region where the curve lies below \(E\). Because \(E\) is below zero, the curve rises above \(E\) at large separations, so the system is bound.

questions.stem: A uniform chain of length \(L\) lies on a frictionless table with one third of its length hanging over the edge, as shown, and is released from rest. What is its speed when the last link leaves the table?
questions.explanation: Take the tabletop as zero. Initially the hanging third has \(U=-\dfrac{M}{3}g\dfrac{L}{6}=-\dfrac{MgL}{18}\); finally the whole chain hangs with \(U=-\dfrac{MgL}{2}\). The kinetic energy gained is \(\dfrac{4}{9}MgL=\tfrac{1}{2}Mv^2\). Each part of the chain falls a different distance, so the center of mass must be tracked.

questions.stem: A car of mass \(m\) moves on a level road with its engine delivering constant power \(P\). The only resistive force is drag of magnitude \(bv\). What is the car's top speed?
questions.explanation: At top speed the driving force equals the drag, and the power delivered is \(Fv=bv\cdot v=bv^2\). Setting \(bv^2=P\) gives the result. The mass affects how quickly the car approaches top speed, not the speed itself.

questions.stem: A planet of radius \(R\) has uniform density \(\rho\). Which expression gives the escape speed from its surface?
questions.explanation: Escape speed is \(\sqrt{\dfrac{2GM}{R}}\) with \(M=\tfrac{4}{3}\pi R^3\rho\), which simplifies to \(R\sqrt{\dfrac{8\pi G\rho}{3}}\). For planets of the same density, escape speed is proportional to radius.

questions.stem: A block attached to a horizontal spring of spring constant \(k\) is pulled a distance \(x_0\) from equilibrium on a floor with coefficient of kinetic friction \(\mu_k\), and released from rest. Where does the block reach its maximum speed during its first motion toward equilibrium?
choices: At a distance \(\dfrac{\mu_kmg}{k}\) from equilibrium, on the side from which it was released
questions.explanation: The speed is greatest where the net force, and so the acceleration, is zero. While the block moves toward equilibrium, friction opposes the spring force, and they balance where \(kx=\mu_kmg\), before the block reaches equilibrium.

questions.stem: A force \(\vec F=2xy\,\hat\imath+x^2\,\hat\jmath\), in newtons with \(x\) and \(y\) in meters, acts on a particle that moves from the origin to the point \((2\text{ m},3\text{ m})\). How much work does the force do?
choices: It depends on the path taken.
questions.explanation: The force is conservative with \(U=-x^2y\), since \(-\dfrac{\partial U}{\partial x}=2xy\) and \(-\dfrac{\partial U}{\partial y}=x^2\). The work is \(U(0,0)-U(2,3)=0-(-12)=12\text{ J}\) for every path.

questions.stem: A \(2.0\text{ kg}\) block slides from rest down a frictionless track shaped like a quarter of a circle of radius \(1.8\text{ m}\), starting level with the circle's center. Using \(g=10\text{ m/s}^2\), what normal force does the track exert on the block at the bottom?
questions.explanation: Falling a height \(R\) gives \(v^2=2gR\). At the bottom, \(N-mg=\dfrac{mv^2}{R}=2mg\), so \(N=3mg=60\text{ N}\), independent of the radius.

questions.stem: A person crouches and then jumps straight up. While the person's feet are in contact with the floor, how much work does the floor's normal force do on the person, and where does the person's kinetic energy come from?
choices: The floor does no work, because the point where the force acts does not move; the energy comes from chemical energy in the person's muscles.
The floor does positive work equal to the person's kinetic energy at takeoff.
The floor does negative work, which is converted into kinetic energy.
The floor does positive work equal to the person's weight times the crouch depth.
questions.explanation: Work requires a displacement of the point of application, and the soles of the feet stay at rest on the floor. The normal force supplies the impulse that changes the person's momentum, but the energy comes from inside the system.

questions.stem: Ignoring air resistance and the planet's rotation, how does the escape speed from a planet's surface depend on the direction in which an object is launched?
choices: It is least when the object is launched straight up.
It is least when the object is launched horizontally.
It does not depend on the direction, because escape depends only on the total energy.
It is greatest when the object is launched straight up.
questions.explanation: An object escapes if its total mechanical energy is zero or positive, \(\tfrac{1}{2}mv^2-\dfrac{GMm}{R}\ge 0\). Kinetic energy depends only on speed, so direction does not matter, provided the path does not intersect the planet.

questions.stem: A satellite in a circular orbit fires its engine briefly several times so that it ends in a higher circular orbit. How do its speed and total mechanical energy compare with their original values?
choices: Its speed is lower, and its total mechanical energy is greater.
Its speed and total mechanical energy are both greater.
Its speed is greater, and its total mechanical energy is lower.
Its speed and total mechanical energy are both lower.
questions.explanation: For a circular orbit, \(v=\sqrt{\dfrac{GM}{r}}\) and \(E=-\dfrac{GMm}{2r}\). A larger radius gives a smaller speed but a less negative, larger total energy: the engine's work increases the potential energy by more than the kinetic energy decreases.

questions.stem: A box is pushed across a rough floor from point A to point B along two different paths, one straight and one curved. Which statement about the work done on the box is correct?
choices: Friction does the same work on both paths, because the endpoints are the same.
Gravity does more work on the curved path.
The total work is the same on both paths, because the box starts and ends at rest.
The work done by gravity is the same for both paths, but friction does more negative work along the longer path.
questions.explanation: Gravity is conservative, so its work depends only on the endpoints, and on a level floor it is zero. Kinetic friction always opposes the motion, so its work is proportional to the path length. A potential energy can be defined only for forces whose work is path-independent.

questions.stem: A \(4\text{ kg}\) object at rest is acted on by a net force \(F(t)=12t-3t^2\), in newtons, from \(t=0\) to \(t=4\text{ s}\). What is its speed at \(t=4\text{ s}\)?
questions.explanation: The impulse is \(\displaystyle\int_0^4\left(12t-3t^2\right)dt=\left[6t^2-t^3\right]_0^4=96-64=32\text{ N}\cdot\text{s}\). Dividing by the mass gives \(8\text{ m/s}\). The force is zero at \(t=4\text{ s}\), but the momentum it has delivered is not.

questions.stem: A thin rod of length \(L\) lies along the \(x\)-axis from \(x=0\) to \(x=L\). Its linear mass density is \(\lambda(x)=cx\), where \(c\) is a constant. Where is the rod's center of mass?
questions.explanation: \(x_{\text{cm}}=\dfrac{\int_0^Lx\,(cx)\,dx}{\int_0^Lcx\,dx}=\dfrac{cL^3/3}{cL^2/2}=\dfrac{2L}{3}\). The rod is denser toward \(x=L\), so the center of mass lies beyond the midpoint.

questions.stem: Three particles are located in the \(xy\)-plane: mass \(m\) at the origin, mass \(2m\) at \((3\text{ m},0)\), and mass \(3m\) at \((0,4\text{ m})\). What are the coordinates of the center of mass?
questions.explanation: \(x_{\text{cm}}=\dfrac{(2m)(3)}{6m}=1\text{ m}\) and \(y_{\text{cm}}=\dfrac{(3m)(4)}{6m}=2\text{ m}\). Each coordinate is a mass-weighted average that includes the particle at the origin in the total mass.

questions.stem: A rocket in deep space ejects exhaust at speed \(v_{\text{ex}}\) relative to the rocket. It starts from rest and burns fuel until its mass is \(\dfrac{1}{e^2}\) of its initial mass. What is its final speed?
questions.explanation: Momentum conservation for the rocket and its exhaust gives \(\Delta v=v_{\text{ex}}\ln\dfrac{m_0}{m}\). With \(\dfrac{m_0}{m}=e^2\), \(\Delta v=2v_{\text{ex}}\). A rocket can exceed its exhaust speed.

questions.stem: A rocket fires its engine in deep space, far from any other objects. Which statement about the system consisting of the rocket and all of the exhaust it has ejected is correct?
choices: The center of mass of the system accelerates in the direction the rocket moves.
The total momentum of the system increases as the rocket speeds up.
The center of mass of the system continues to move with the velocity it had before the engine fired.
The total kinetic energy of the system stays constant.
questions.explanation: No external force acts on the system, so its total momentum and the velocity of its center of mass do not change. The rocket gains forward momentum and the exhaust gains equal backward momentum. Kinetic energy increases as chemical energy is released.

questions.stem: A block of mass \(m\) moving with speed \(v\) collides elastically and head-on with a block of mass \(3m\) that is at rest. What fraction of the first block's kinetic energy is transferred to the second block?
questions.explanation: The struck block leaves with speed \(\dfrac{2m}{m+3m}v=\dfrac{v}{2}\), so its kinetic energy is \(\tfrac{1}{2}(3m)\dfrac{v^2}{4}=\dfrac{3}{4}\left(\tfrac{1}{2}mv^2\right)\). In general the fraction transferred is \(\dfrac{4m_1m_2}{(m_1+m_2)^2}\), which is greatest when the masses are equal.

questions.stem: An open cart of mass \(M\) rolls without friction at speed \(v_0\). Sand is dropped vertically into the cart until a mass \(m\) of sand has collected. What is the speed of the cart afterward?
questions.explanation: The sand arrives with no horizontal momentum, and no horizontal external force acts, so \(Mv_0=(M+m)v\). Kinetic energy is not conserved, because the sand comes to rest relative to the cart through friction; assuming it is gives the square-root expression.

questions.skill: Force from a stream of matter
questions.stem: A horizontal jet of water with density \(\rho\), cross-sectional area \(A\), and speed \(v\) strikes a wall and runs straight down the wall without splashing back. What is the magnitude of the force the water exerts on the wall?
questions.explanation: Mass reaches the wall at the rate \(\dfrac{dm}{dt}=\rho Av\), and each bit of water loses horizontal momentum \(v\) per unit mass. The force is the rate of change of momentum, \(\rho Av\cdot v=\rho Av^2\). If the water rebounded at speed \(v\), the force would be twice as large.

questions.stem: The graph shows the net force exerted on an object as a function of time. What is the average net force on the object during the interval from \(t=0\) to \(t=6\text{ s}\)?
questions.explanation: The average force is the impulse divided by the time. The impulse is the area under the graph, \(40+80+40=160\text{ N}\cdot\text{s}\), so the average is \(\dfrac{160}{6}\approx 27\text{ N}\).

questions.stem: A projectile is launched over level ground and would land a horizontal distance \(R\) from the launch point. At the top of its path it explodes into two pieces of equal mass. One piece is brought to rest by the explosion and falls straight down. How far from the launch point does the other piece land?
questions.explanation: The explosion is internal, so the center of mass still lands at \(R\). Both pieces land at the same time, because the explosion gives them no vertical velocity. One lands at \(\dfrac{R}{2}\), so the other must land at \(\dfrac{3R}{2}\) for the midpoint to be at \(R\).

questions.stem: A ball is dropped from height \(h\) onto a floor. In each bounce it leaves the floor with half the speed it had just before impact. Air resistance is negligible. To what maximum height does it rise after its second bounce?
questions.explanation: The maximum height is proportional to the square of the speed leaving the floor. Each bounce halves the speed and so reduces the height to one fourth. After two bounces the height is \(\dfrac{h}{16}\).

questions.stem: Two objects collide elastically. In the reference frame of their center of mass, which statement describes the collision?
choices: The total momentum is zero, and both objects are at rest after the collision.
The total kinetic energy is zero before and after the collision.
Each object's velocity is unchanged by the collision.
The total momentum is zero, and each object leaves with the same speed it had before the collision.
questions.explanation: In the center-of-mass frame the momenta are always equal and opposite. For the kinetic energy to be conserved as well, the magnitudes of the momenta cannot change, so each object keeps its speed and only its direction of motion changes. If both objects came to rest, the collision would be perfectly inelastic.

questions.stem: Two blocks of mass \(m\) connected by a spring of spring constant \(k\) rest on a frictionless surface, as shown, with the spring at its natural length. One block is suddenly given a velocity \(v\) toward the other. What is the maximum compression of the spring?
questions.explanation: At maximum compression the blocks have the same velocity, \(\dfrac{v}{2}\), by momentum conservation. The kinetic energy is then \(\tfrac{1}{2}(2m)\left(\tfrac{v}{2}\right)^2=\tfrac{1}{4}mv^2\), so \(\tfrac{1}{2}kx^2=\tfrac{1}{2}mv^2-\tfrac{1}{4}mv^2\) and \(x=v\sqrt{\dfrac{m}{2k}}\). Assuming all of the kinetic energy is stored gives \(v\sqrt{\dfrac{m}{k}}\).

questions.stem: A puck sliding on frictionless ice strikes an identical puck at rest in a glancing, elastic collision. What is the angle between the velocities of the two pucks after the collision?
choices: It depends on the initial speed of the moving puck.
questions.explanation: With equal masses, momentum conservation gives \(\vec v=\vec v_1+\vec v_2\) and energy conservation gives \(v^2=v_1^2+v_2^2\). Squaring the first equation and comparing shows \(\vec v_1\cdot\vec v_2=0\), so the final velocities are perpendicular.

questions.explanation: With \(V=\dfrac{mv}{m+M}\), the final kinetic energy is \(\dfrac{(mv)^2}{2(m+M)}\), which divided by \(\tfrac{1}{2}mv^2\) is \(\dfrac{m}{m+M}\). For a light bullet nearly all of the energy is dissipated in the block.

questions.stem: The block in the figure slides from rest down the frictionless wedge, which is free to move on the frictionless floor. When the block reaches the floor it moves horizontally with speed \(v\) relative to the ground. What is the speed of the wedge then?
questions.explanation: No horizontal external force acts on the block and wedge together, so their total horizontal momentum stays zero: \(mv-MV=0\). The wedge moves opposite to the block with speed \(\dfrac{mv}{M}\).

questions.stem: The block in the figure slides down the frictionless wedge, which is free to move on the frictionless floor. For the system of the block, the wedge, and Earth, which quantities are conserved?
choices: The total momentum of the block and wedge in all directions
The horizontal momentum of the block and wedge only; mechanical energy is lost as the wedge moves
Mechanical energy only; momentum changes because the wedge pushes the block
The horizontal momentum of the block and wedge and the total mechanical energy
questions.explanation: Gravity and the normal force from the floor are vertical, so the horizontal momentum of the block and wedge is conserved but their vertical momentum is not. No friction acts anywhere, so mechanical energy is conserved.

questions.stem: A \(5000\text{ kg}\) rocket on a launch pad ejects exhaust at \(30\text{ kg/s}\) with a speed of \(2000\text{ m/s}\) relative to the rocket. Using \(g=10\text{ m/s}^2\), what is its upward acceleration just after liftoff?
questions.explanation: The thrust is the rate at which momentum is carried away by the exhaust, \(\left(30\right)\left(2000\right)=6.0\times 10^4\text{ N}\). Subtracting the weight of \(5.0\times 10^4\text{ N}\) gives a net force of \(1.0\times 10^4\text{ N}\) and an acceleration of \(2.0\text{ m/s}^2\).

questions.skill: Center of mass of an extended object
questions.stem: A circular hole of radius \(\dfrac{R}{2}\) is cut from a uniform disk of radius \(R\). The center of the hole is a distance \(\dfrac{R}{2}\) from the center of the disk. Where is the center of mass of the remaining piece?
choices: A distance \(\dfrac{R}{4}\) from the disk's center, on the side opposite the hole
A distance \(\dfrac{R}{6}\) from the disk's center, on the side opposite the hole
A distance \(\dfrac{R}{2}\) from the disk's center, on the side opposite the hole
questions.explanation: Treat the hole as negative mass. It has one fourth of the disk's area, so the remaining piece has three fourths: \(x_{\text{cm}}=\dfrac{0-\tfrac{1}{4}\left(\tfrac{R}{2}\right)}{\tfrac{3}{4}}=-\dfrac{R}{6}\).

questions.stem: A force \(F(t)=F_0\sin\!\left(\dfrac{\pi t}{T}\right)\) acts on an object from \(t=0\) to \(t=T\). What impulse does it deliver?
questions.explanation: \(J=\displaystyle\int_0^TF_0\sin\!\left(\dfrac{\pi t}{T}\right)dt=\dfrac{F_0T}{\pi}\left[-\cos\!\left(\dfrac{\pi t}{T}\right)\right]_0^T=\dfrac{2F_0T}{\pi}\). The average force is \(\dfrac{2}{\pi}F_0\), about 64 percent of the peak.

questions.stem: Sand falls vertically onto a conveyor belt at a rate \(\lambda\), in kilograms per second, and the belt moves at a constant speed \(v\). What power must the motor supply to keep the belt moving at that speed?
questions.explanation: The belt must give horizontal momentum to the sand at the rate \(\lambda v\), which is the force required, and the power is that force times \(v\). Only half of this power becomes kinetic energy of the sand; the other half is dissipated as the sand slips before matching the belt's speed.

questions.stem: A small ball of mass \(m\) rests on top of a large ball of mass \(3m\), and the two are dropped together from height \(h\) onto a hard floor. Assume all collisions are elastic and the large ball rebounds from the floor before it strikes the small ball. How high does the small ball rise?
questions.explanation: Both balls reach the floor at speed \(v\). The large ball rebounds upward at \(v\) and meets the small ball still moving down at \(v\). An elastic collision with a mass ratio of 3 stops the large ball and sends the small ball up at \(2v\), which carries it to \(4h\).

questions.stem: An object at rest explodes into three pieces. A piece of mass \(m\) moves east at speed \(v\), a second piece of mass \(m\) moves north at speed \(v\), and the third piece has mass \(2m\). What is the speed of the third piece?
questions.explanation: The total momentum stays zero, so the third piece's momentum cancels the sum of the other two, which has magnitude \(\sqrt{2}\,mv\). Dividing by \(2m\) gives \(\dfrac{\sqrt{2}}{2}v\), directed southwest.

questions.stem: In test 1, a car hits a rigid wall at speed \(v\) and stops. In test 2, an identical car traveling at speed \(v\) hits a second identical car traveling toward it at speed \(v\), and both stop. How does the force on the first car compare in the two tests?
choices: It is twice as great in test 2, because the relative speed is \(2v\).
It is about the same, because in both tests the car stops from speed \(v\) in about the same time.
It is half as great in test 2, because the other car absorbs half the impact.
It is four times as great in test 2, because the kinetic energy is four times greater.
questions.explanation: In both tests the car's change in momentum is \(mv\). By symmetry, the head-on collision is equivalent to each car hitting a rigid wall at the point where they meet, so the stopping time and the force are about the same.

questions.stem: A block slides onto a cart that rolls on a frictionless track, and friction between the block and the cart slows the block until the two move together. For the block–cart system, what is conserved?
choices: Kinetic energy is conserved, but momentum is not.
Momentum is conserved, but kinetic energy is not.
Both momentum and kinetic energy are conserved.
Neither momentum nor kinetic energy is conserved, because friction acts.
questions.explanation: The friction between block and cart is internal to the system, so it cannot change the total momentum. It does convert kinetic energy into internal energy, as in any perfectly inelastic collision.

questions.stem: A batter keeps the bat in contact with the ball for a longer time while applying the same average force. What is the effect on the ball?
choices: Its change in momentum is unchanged, because the average force is unchanged.
Its change in momentum is smaller, because the force is spread over more time.
Its kinetic energy is unchanged, because the bat's speed is unchanged.
Its change in momentum is greater, because the impulse is greater.
questions.explanation: Impulse is the average force multiplied by the contact time, and impulse equals the change in momentum. A longer contact at the same force delivers more momentum, which is the reason for following through.

questions.stem: A person standing at rest in a boat on still water jumps off with the same speed relative to the water in two trials, once horizontally and once at \(45^\circ\) above the horizontal. Ignoring water resistance, in which trial does the boat move backward faster?
choices: When the person jumps horizontally, because more horizontal momentum is given to the person
When the person jumps at \(45^\circ\), because the person pushes down on the boat
The boat's speed is the same, because the person's speed is the same
The boat does not move in either trial, because the water holds it in place
questions.explanation: Only horizontal momentum is conserved, since the water and gravity exert vertical forces. A horizontal jump gives the person all of the momentum horizontally; at \(45^\circ\) only \(\cos 45^\circ\) of it is horizontal, so the boat recoils less.

questions.stem: When a rifle is fired, the bullet and the rifle receive momenta of equal magnitude. How do their kinetic energies compare?
choices: They have equal kinetic energies, because their momenta are equal.
The rifle has more kinetic energy, because it is more massive.
The bullet has far more kinetic energy, because kinetic energy is \(\dfrac{p^2}{2m}\) and its mass is much smaller.
The bullet has more kinetic energy, but only because it moves faster than sound.
questions.explanation: For equal momenta, kinetic energy is inversely proportional to mass. A bullet with a thousandth of the rifle's mass gets about a thousand times as much kinetic energy, which is why a rifle's recoil is survivable.

questions.stem: A thin rod of mass \(M\) and length \(L\) lies along the \(x\)-axis from \(x=0\) to \(x=L\), with linear mass density \(\lambda(x)=cx\). What is its rotational inertia about an axis through \(x=0\) perpendicular to the rod?
questions.explanation: The mass is \(M=\displaystyle\int_0^Lcx\,dx=\dfrac{cL^2}{2}\), and \(I=\displaystyle\int_0^Lx^2(cx)\,dx=\dfrac{cL^4}{4}=\dfrac{1}{2}ML^2\). It exceeds the uniform-rod value \(\dfrac{1}{3}ML^2\) because more of the mass is far from the axis.

questions.stem: A uniform disk of mass \(M\) and radius \(R\) has rotational inertia \(\tfrac{1}{2}MR^2\) about the axis through its center perpendicular to its face. What is its rotational inertia about a parallel axis through a point on its rim?
questions.explanation: The parallel-axis theorem gives \(I=I_{\text{cm}}+Md^2=\tfrac{1}{2}MR^2+MR^2=\dfrac{3}{2}MR^2\), where \(d=R\) is the distance between the axes.

questions.stem: The pulley shown is a uniform disk of mass \(M\) and radius \(R\), with rotational inertia \(\tfrac{1}{2}MR^2\), on a frictionless axle. Suppose the string passes over the pulley without slipping and supports a block of mass \(m_1\) on one side and a block of mass \(m_2>m_1\) on the other. What is the magnitude of the blocks' acceleration?
questions.explanation: For the blocks, \(m_2g-T_2=m_2a\) and \(T_1-m_1g=m_1a\). For the pulley, \((T_2-T_1)R=\tfrac{1}{2}MR^2\dfrac{a}{R}\). Adding the equations gives \((m_2-m_1)g=\left(m_1+m_2+\tfrac{1}{2}M\right)a\). The pulley adds an effective inertia of \(\dfrac{I}{R^2}\).

questions.stem: A force \(\vec F=3\,\hat\imath+4\,\hat\jmath\), in newtons, acts at the point \(\vec r=2\,\hat\imath\), in meters, relative to the origin. What is the torque about the origin?
questions.explanation: \(\vec\tau=\vec r\times\vec F=(2\,\hat\imath)\times(3\,\hat\imath+4\,\hat\jmath)=8\,(\hat\imath\times\hat\jmath)=8\,\hat k\). The component of the force along \(\vec r\) contributes nothing.

questions.stem: A wheel has angular acceleration \(\alpha(t)=6t\), in \(\text{rad/s}^2\), and an angular velocity of \(2\text{ rad/s}\) at \(t=0\). Through what angle does it turn between \(t=0\) and \(t=2\text{ s}\)?
questions.explanation: Integrating, \(\omega(t)=3t^2+2\) and \(\theta(t)=t^3+2t\). At \(t=2\text{ s}\), \(\theta=8+4=12\text{ rad}\). The angular velocity at that time is \(14\text{ rad/s}\).

questions.stem: A uniform rod of mass \(M\) and length \(L\), with rotational inertia \(\tfrac{1}{3}ML^2\) about its end, is held horizontally and released, as shown. What is the magnitude of the linear acceleration of the free end of the rod immediately after release?
questions.explanation: The torque about the pivot is \(Mg\dfrac{L}{2}\), so \(\alpha=\dfrac{MgL/2}{ML^2/3}=\dfrac{3g}{2L}\). The free end has acceleration \(\alpha L=\dfrac{3}{2}g\), which is greater than \(g\). The center of mass has acceleration \(\dfrac{3}{4}g\).

questions.stem: A coin rests on the rod shown, at the free end, and the rod is released from rest in the horizontal position. Which statement describes what happens immediately after release?
choices: The coin stays in contact with the rod, because both fall with acceleration \(g\).
The coin stays in contact with the rod, because the rod accelerates more slowly than \(g\).
The coin slides toward the pivot, because the rod tilts.
The coin loses contact with the rod, because the end of the rod accelerates downward faster than \(g\).
questions.explanation: Points on the rod at a distance \(r\) from the pivot have acceleration \(\alpha r=\dfrac{3g}{2L}r\). This exceeds \(g\) for \(r>\dfrac{2L}{3}\), so the end of the rod falls away from the coin, which can accelerate at no more than \(g\).

questions.stem: A uniform solid sphere, with rotational inertia \(\tfrac{2}{5}MR^2\), rolls without slipping down a ramp inclined at angle \(\theta\), as shown. What is the minimum coefficient of static friction required?
questions.explanation: The equations \(Mg\sin\theta-f=Ma\) and \(fR=\tfrac{2}{5}MR^2\dfrac{a}{R}\) give \(a=\dfrac{5}{7}g\sin\theta\) and \(f=\dfrac{2}{7}Mg\sin\theta\). Requiring \(f\le\mu_sMg\cos\theta\) gives \(\mu_s\ge\dfrac{2}{7}\tan\theta\).

questions.skill: Rotational dynamics with a resistive torque
questions.stem: A flywheel with rotational inertia \(I\) spins with angular velocity \(\omega_0\). At \(t=0\) the only torque on it becomes a resistive torque of magnitude \(b\omega\), where \(b\) is a constant. Which expression gives its angular velocity at later times?
questions.explanation: \(I\dfrac{d\omega}{dt}=-b\omega\) separates to \(\dfrac{d\omega}{\omega}=-\dfrac{b}{I}dt\), which integrates to \(\omega=\omega_0e^{-bt/I}\). A linear decrease would require a constant torque.

questions.stem: A uniform horizontal rod of mass \(M\) is attached to a wall by a hinge and supported by a cable at \(30^\circ\) to the rod, as shown. A sign of mass \(M\) hangs from the end where the cable is attached. What is the magnitude of the force the hinge exerts on the rod?
questions.explanation: Torques about the hinge give \(T\sin 30^\circ L=Mg\dfrac{L}{2}+MgL\), so \(T=3Mg\). The hinge force has horizontal component \(T\cos 30^\circ=\dfrac{3\sqrt{3}}{2}Mg\) and vertical component \(2Mg-T\sin 30^\circ=\tfrac{1}{2}Mg\). The magnitude is \(Mg\sqrt{\tfrac{27}{4}+\tfrac{1}{4}}=\sqrt{7}\,Mg\).

questions.stem: Which integral gives the rotational inertia of a uniform disk of mass \(M\) and radius \(R\) about the axis through its center perpendicular to its face?
questions.explanation: Divide the disk into thin rings of radius \(r\) and width \(dr\). Each ring has mass \(dm=\dfrac{M}{\pi R^2}(2\pi r\,dr)=\dfrac{2M}{R^2}r\,dr\) and rotational inertia \(r^2\,dm\). Integrating gives \(\tfrac{1}{2}MR^2\).

questions.stem: A uniform box of width \(w\) and height \(h\) rests on a rough floor. A horizontal force applied at the top edge of the box is slowly increased. Under what condition on the coefficient of static friction \(\mu_s\) does the box tip before it slides?
questions.explanation: The box begins to tip about its lower far edge when \(Fh=mg\dfrac{w}{2}\), that is, at \(F=\dfrac{mgw}{2h}\). It begins to slide at \(F=\mu_smg\). Tipping comes first if \(\dfrac{mgw}{2h}<\mu_smg\). Tall, narrow boxes tip easily.

questions.stem: A hoop, a uniform disk, and a uniform solid sphere have the same mass and the same radius. Each rotates about an axis through its center (for the hoop and the disk, the axis perpendicular to its plane). Which lists the objects in order of increasing rotational inertia?
choices: They are equal, because the masses and radii are equal.
questions.explanation: Rotational inertia depends on how far the mass is from the axis. All of the hoop's mass is at distance \(R\), giving \(MR^2\). The disk, \(\tfrac{1}{2}MR^2\), has mass distributed from the center outward, and the sphere, \(\tfrac{2}{5}MR^2\), has even more of its mass near the axis.

questions.stem: The axle of a rapidly spinning wheel is horizontal and is supported at only one end. Instead of falling, the wheel's axle slowly sweeps around in a horizontal circle. Which statement best explains this motion?
choices: The spinning wheel is not acted on by gravity.
The torque due to gravity is parallel to the angular momentum, so it increases the wheel's spin.
The torque due to gravity is perpendicular to the wheel's angular momentum, so it changes the direction of the angular momentum without changing its magnitude.
The support exerts a torque that exactly cancels the torque due to gravity.
questions.explanation: Torque is the rate of change of angular momentum, \(\vec\tau=\dfrac{d\vec L}{dt}\). Gravity's torque about the support is horizontal and perpendicular to \(\vec L\), which lies along the axle, so \(\vec L\) changes direction continuously and the axle precesses.

questions.stem: A uniform ladder of mass \(M\) and length \(L\) leans against a frictionless wall at angle \(\theta\) with the floor, as shown. A person of mass \(M\) stands three quarters of the way up. What force does the wall exert on the ladder?
questions.explanation: Taking torques about the base: \(N_wL\sin\theta=Mg\dfrac{L}{2}\cos\theta+Mg\dfrac{3L}{4}\cos\theta=\dfrac{5}{4}MgL\cos\theta\). The floor's friction must equal this force, so a person climbing higher makes the ladder more likely to slip.

questions.stem: The spool shown, of mass \(M\), outer radius \(R\), inner radius \(r\), and rotational inertia \(I\) about its center, is pulled by the horizontal force \(F\) and rolls without slipping. What is the acceleration of its center?
questions.explanation: Taking torques about the contact point, where the unknown friction force exerts none, the string's line of action is a height \(R-r\) above the ground: \(F(R-r)=\left(I+MR^2\right)\alpha\), with \(a=R\alpha\). The rotational inertia about the contact point comes from the parallel-axis theorem.

questions.stem: The spool shown rests on a rough surface and is pulled gently by the horizontal force \(F\) applied at the bottom of its hub. Which way does it roll?
choices: To the left, away from the pull, unwinding the string
It does not move, because the torque and force cancel
To the right, toward the pull, winding up the string
To the right, but it slides without rotating
questions.explanation: About the contact point, the string's line of action lies above the ground by \(R-r\), so its torque turns the spool clockwise about that point, which rolls it to the right. The string winds onto the hub because the hub rotates the same way.

questions.skill: Rotational dynamics of a pivoted rod
questions.stem: A uniform rod of mass \(M\) and length \(L\) is pivoted at a point \(\dfrac{L}{4}\) from one end and held horizontally. Its rotational inertia about its center is \(\tfrac{1}{12}ML^2\). What is its angular acceleration immediately after release?
questions.explanation: By the parallel-axis theorem, \(I=\tfrac{1}{12}ML^2+M\left(\tfrac{L}{4}\right)^2=\tfrac{7}{48}ML^2\). The torque of gravity is \(Mg\dfrac{L}{4}\), so \(\alpha=\dfrac{MgL/4}{7ML^2/48}=\dfrac{12g}{7L}\).

questions.stem: The pulley in the system shown has rotational inertia \(I\) and radius \(R\), and the string does not slip on it. The ramp and axle are frictionless, and \(m_2\) descends. What is the magnitude of the acceleration of the blocks?
questions.explanation: For the blocks, \(m_2g-T_2=m_2a\) and \(T_1-m_1g\sin\theta=m_1a\); for the pulley, \((T_2-T_1)R=I\dfrac{a}{R}\). Adding the three equations eliminates the tensions. The pulley acts like an additional mass \(\dfrac{I}{R^2}\) to be accelerated.

questions.stem: A flywheel turning at \(30\text{ rad/s}\) slows to a stop at a constant rate in \(10\text{ s}\). About how many revolutions does it make while stopping?
questions.explanation: With constant angular acceleration, the angle turned is the average angular speed times the time: \(15(10)=150\text{ rad}\), which is \(\dfrac{150}{2\pi}\approx 24\) revolutions.

questions.skill: Rotational inertia of a composite object
questions.stem: A uniform rod of mass \(M\) and length \(L\) has a small ball of mass \(M\) attached to each end. What is the rotational inertia of the assembly about an axis through the rod's center, perpendicular to the rod?
questions.explanation: Rotational inertias about the same axis add: the rod contributes \(\tfrac{1}{12}ML^2\) and each ball \(M\left(\tfrac{L}{2}\right)^2=\tfrac{1}{4}ML^2\). The total is \(\left(\tfrac{1}{12}+\tfrac{1}{2}\right)ML^2\).

questions.stem: A thin disk of mass \(M\) and radius \(R\) has a surface mass density that increases linearly with distance from its center, \(\sigma=cr\). What is its rotational inertia about the axis through its center perpendicular to its face?
questions.explanation: Using rings of area \(2\pi r\,dr\): \(M=\displaystyle\int_0^Rcr\,2\pi r\,dr=\dfrac{2\pi cR^3}{3}\) and \(I=\displaystyle\int_0^Rr^2\,cr\,2\pi r\,dr=\dfrac{2\pi cR^5}{5}\). The ratio gives \(\tfrac{3}{5}MR^2\), more than a uniform disk because the mass is concentrated toward the rim.

questions.stem: A gyroscope with rotational inertia \(I\) spins with angular speed \(\omega\). Its axle is horizontal and is supported at a point a distance \(r\) from its center of mass. Its total mass is \(m\). What is its rate of precession?
questions.explanation: Gravity's torque about the support, \(mgr\), is perpendicular to the angular momentum \(I\omega\), so it rotates that vector without changing its size. The angular momentum turns at the rate \(\Omega=\dfrac{\tau}{L}\). A faster spin gives a slower precession.

questions.stem: A rod on a frictionless horizontal surface is acted on by two forces of equal magnitude in opposite directions that do not act along the same line. Which statement is correct?
choices: The rod is in equilibrium, because the forces cancel.
The net force and net torque are both zero.
The net force is zero but the net torque is not, so the rod is not in equilibrium.
The net torque is zero but the net force is not.
questions.explanation: Equal and opposite forces with different lines of action form a couple. Their torque is the same about every point and equals the force times the distance between the lines, so the rod's rotation speeds up while its center of mass stays put.

questions.stem: How does the rotational inertia of a uniform rod about an axis through one end compare with its rotational inertia about a parallel axis through its center?
choices: It is the same, because the mass and length are the same.
It is four times as large.
questions.explanation: About the center, \(I=\tfrac{1}{12}ML^2\); about the end, \(\tfrac{1}{3}ML^2\). Rotational inertia depends on how far the mass lies from the chosen axis, and the center-of-mass axis always gives the smallest value among parallel axes.

questions.stem: Earth rotates from west to east. In what direction does its angular velocity vector point?
choices: Eastward, in the direction of the rotation
Toward the North Star, along the axis from the South Pole to the North Pole
questions.explanation: By the right-hand rule, with the fingers curling west to east, the thumb points along the axis toward the north. The angular velocity vector lies along the axis of rotation, not in the plane of the motion.

questions.stem: A ball rolls without slipping down an incline. Which statement about the static friction force on it is correct?
choices: Its magnitude is whatever is needed to keep the ball rolling, which can be less than \(\mu_sN\).
It is zero, because the contact point does not slide.
It points down the incline, because the ball speeds up.
questions.explanation: Static friction adjusts to prevent sliding, up to a maximum of \(\mu_sN\). For a sphere it is \(\tfrac{2}{7}mg\sin\theta\), directed up the incline; the ball slips only if that required value exceeds \(\mu_sN\).

questions.stem: A yo-yo is released from rest with its string held fixed, and it falls as the string unwinds. How does the tension in the string compare with the yo-yo's weight?
choices: It is less than the weight, because the yo-yo's center accelerates downward.
It equals the weight, because the string supports the yo-yo.
It is greater than the weight, because the string must also spin the yo-yo.
It is zero, because the yo-yo falls freely.
questions.explanation: The net force on the yo-yo is downward, so the tension is less than \(mg\). Its torque about the center still spins the yo-yo, which is why the acceleration is less than \(g\).

questions.stem: A uniform rod of mass \(M\) and length \(L\), with rotational inertia \(\tfrac{1}{3}ML^2\) about its end, is released from rest in the horizontal position shown. What is the speed of its free end as the rod passes through the vertical position?
questions.explanation: The center of mass falls a distance \(\dfrac{L}{2}\), so \(Mg\dfrac{L}{2}=\tfrac{1}{2}\left(\tfrac{1}{3}ML^2\right)\omega^2\) and \(\omega=\sqrt{\dfrac{3g}{L}}\). The free end moves at \(\omega L=\sqrt{3gL}\). A point mass falling a distance \(L\) would reach \(\sqrt{2gL}\).

questions.stem: A thin hoop rolls without slipping along a level floor with speed \(v\) and then rolls without slipping up a ramp. What maximum height does its center rise?
questions.explanation: A hoop has \(I=MR^2\), so its rotational kinetic energy, \(\tfrac{1}{2}MR^2\dfrac{v^2}{R^2}\), equals its translational kinetic energy. The total is \(Mv^2=Mgh\), so \(h=\dfrac{v^2}{g}\), twice the height reached by a sliding block.

questions.stem: A particle of mass \(m\) moves with constant velocity \(v\) along the line \(y=b\), parallel to the \(x\)-axis. What is the magnitude of its angular momentum about the origin?
choices: \(mv\sqrt{x^2+b^2}\), increasing as the particle moves away
Zero, because the particle moves in a straight line
questions.explanation: \(L=|\vec r\times\vec p|=mvr\sin\phi\), and \(r\sin\phi\) is the perpendicular distance from the origin to the line of motion, which is \(b\). No torque acts on the particle, so its angular momentum is constant even though it does not move in a circle.
