questions.stem: A lump of clay of mass \(m\) moving with speed \(v\) strikes and sticks to the free end of a rod of mass \(3m\) and length \(L\) that is pivoted at its other end, as shown. The rod's rotational inertia about the pivot is \(\tfrac{1}{3}(3m)L^2\). What fraction of the clay's kinetic energy is dissipated in the collision?
questions.explanation: Angular momentum about the pivot gives \(mvL=\left(mL^2+mL^2\right)\omega\), so \(\omega=\dfrac{v}{2L}\). The final kinetic energy is \(\tfrac{1}{2}\left(2mL^2\right)\dfrac{v^2}{4L^2}=\tfrac{1}{4}mv^2\), half of the initial \(\tfrac{1}{2}mv^2\).

questions.stem: A child of mass \(m\) runs with speed \(v\) along a line tangent to the rim of a stationary merry-go-round of radius \(R\) and rotational inertia \(I\), and jumps on at the rim. What is the angular speed of the merry-go-round afterward?
questions.explanation: The child's angular momentum about the axle before landing is \(mvR\). Afterward the child and the merry-go-round rotate together with total rotational inertia \(I+mR^2\), so \(\omega=\dfrac{mvR}{I+mR^2}\).

questions.stem: Kepler's second law states that a line from the Sun to a planet sweeps out equal areas in equal times. This law is a direct consequence of which fact?
choices: The gravitational force on the planet is inversely proportional to the square of the distance.
The mechanical energy of the planet–Sun system is conserved.
The orbit of the planet is an ellipse.
The gravitational force on the planet points along the line to the Sun, so it exerts no torque about the Sun.
questions.explanation: The rate at which area is swept out is \(\dfrac{L}{2m}\), so it is constant whenever the planet's angular momentum about the Sun is constant. That requires only that the force be central. The law would hold for any central force, not only an inverse-square one.

questions.stem: A satellite moves in the elliptical orbit shown around a planet of mass \(M\). What is its speed at its closest point, a distance \(r_1\) from the planet's center?
questions.explanation: Angular momentum conservation gives \(v_2=v_1\dfrac{r_1}{r_2}\). Substituting into energy conservation, \(\tfrac{1}{2}v_1^2-\dfrac{GM}{r_1}=\tfrac{1}{2}v_2^2-\dfrac{GM}{r_2}\), and solving gives \(v_1^2=\dfrac{2GMr_2}{r_1(r_1+r_2)}\). This lies between the circular-orbit speed and the escape speed at \(r_1\).

questions.stem: A bowling ball, a uniform sphere with rotational inertia \(\tfrac{2}{5}MR^2\), is released onto a rough horizontal lane sliding at speed \(v\) without rotating. What is its speed once it is rolling without slipping?
questions.explanation: Friction acts at the point of contact, so it exerts no torque about a point on the lane, and angular momentum about that point is conserved: \(MvR=Mv_fR+\tfrac{2}{5}MR^2\dfrac{v_f}{R}\). This gives \(v_f=\dfrac{5}{7}v\), independent of the coefficient of friction.

questions.stem: A wheel with rotational inertia \(4\text{ kg}\cdot\text{m}^2\) starts from rest and is acted on by a net torque \(\tau(\theta)=3\theta^2\), in newton-meters, as it turns from \(\theta=0\) to \(\theta=2\text{ rad}\). What is its angular speed at \(\theta=2\text{ rad}\)?
questions.explanation: The work done is \(\displaystyle\int_0^23\theta^2\,d\theta=8\text{ J}\). Setting \(\tfrac{1}{2}I\omega^2=8\) gives \(\omega^2=4\), so \(\omega=2\text{ rad/s}\).

questions.stem: A constant net torque \(\tau\) acts on a flywheel of rotational inertia \(I\) that starts from rest. What is the instantaneous power delivered to the flywheel at time \(t\)?
questions.explanation: The angular velocity is \(\omega=\dfrac{\tau t}{I}\), and the power is \(P=\tau\omega=\dfrac{\tau^2t}{I}\). The expression \(\dfrac{\tau^2t^2}{2I}\) is the kinetic energy at time \(t\), and \(\dfrac{\tau^2t}{2I}\) is the average power up to time \(t\).

questions.stem: A puck of mass \(m\) moves in a circle of radius \(r\) with speed \(v\) on a frictionless table, held by a string that passes through a small hole at the center of the circle. The string is slowly pulled down through the hole until the radius is \(\dfrac{r}{2}\). How much work is done on the puck by the string?
choices: Zero, because the tension is perpendicular to the velocity
questions.explanation: The tension points toward the hole and exerts no torque about it, so \(mvr\) is conserved and the speed doubles. The kinetic energy rises from \(\tfrac{1}{2}mv^2\) to \(2mv^2\), so the work done is \(\dfrac{3}{2}mv^2\). While the radius shrinks, the velocity has an inward component, so the tension does do work.

questions.stem: A ball slides and spins along a rough horizontal floor before it begins rolling without slipping. About which point is the ball's angular momentum conserved during the sliding, and why?
choices: A fixed point on the floor along the ball's path, because the friction force acts along a line through that point.
The ball's center of mass, because the weight and normal force act through it.
Any point at all, because friction is an internal force.
No point, because friction always changes angular momentum.
questions.explanation: The friction force acts at the floor and is directed along the floor, so its line of action passes through any point of the floor on the ball's path, and its torque about such a point is zero. The weight and normal force cancel. About the center of mass friction does exert a torque, which changes the ball's spin.

questions.stem: A uniform disk of mass \(M\), with rotational inertia \(\tfrac{1}{2}MR^2\), rolls without slipping with its center moving at speed \(v\). What is its total kinetic energy?
questions.explanation: The kinetic energy is \(\tfrac{1}{2}Mv^2+\tfrac{1}{2}\left(\tfrac{1}{2}MR^2\right)\dfrac{v^2}{R^2}=\tfrac{1}{2}Mv^2+\tfrac{1}{4}Mv^2=\dfrac{3}{4}Mv^2\).

questions.stem: A rod lies at rest on a frictionless horizontal surface and is not attached to anything. A lump of clay sliding on the surface strikes one end of the rod perpendicular to it and sticks. Which statement about the rod–clay system is correct?
choices: Its center of mass moves at constant velocity, and the system also rotates about its center of mass.
Its center of mass remains at rest while the system rotates.
It moves in a straight line without rotating.
It rotates about the end of the rod opposite the clay.
questions.explanation: No external horizontal force acts, so the system's linear momentum is conserved and its center of mass moves at \(\dfrac{mv}{M+m}\). The clay's line of motion does not pass through the center of mass, so the system has angular momentum about it and must rotate as well.

questions.stem: A uniform solid sphere, with rotational inertia \(\tfrac{2}{5}MR^2\), rolls without slipping at speed \(v\) onto an incline like the one shown, at angle \(\theta\), and rolls up it. How far along the incline does it travel before stopping?
questions.explanation: The sphere's kinetic energy, \(\tfrac{1}{2}Mv^2+\tfrac{1}{5}Mv^2=\tfrac{7}{10}Mv^2\), becomes potential energy \(Mgd\sin\theta\). Because the rotational energy also converts, the sphere travels farther than a sliding block would.

questions.stem: The uniform rod shown, pivoted at one end with rotational inertia \(\tfrac{1}{3}ML^2\), is released from rest in the horizontal position. What is its angular speed when it has rotated \(30^\circ\) below the horizontal?
questions.explanation: The center of mass drops \(\dfrac{L}{2}\sin 30^\circ=\dfrac{L}{4}\), so \(\dfrac{MgL}{4}=\tfrac{1}{2}\left(\tfrac{1}{3}ML^2\right)\omega^2\), giving \(\omega^2=\dfrac{3g}{2L}\). Using \(\cos 30^\circ\) for the drop gives the last choice.

questions.stem: A uniform rod of mass \(M\) and length \(L\) spins freely in a horizontal plane at angular speed \(\omega_0\) about a vertical axis through its center. Two beads, each of mass \(m\), start at the center and slide without friction to the ends of the rod. What is the final angular speed?
questions.explanation: Angular momentum is conserved: \(\tfrac{1}{12}ML^2\omega_0=\left(\tfrac{1}{12}ML^2+2m\tfrac{L^2}{4}\right)\omega\). Multiplying by \(\dfrac{12}{L^2}\) gives \(M\omega_0=(M+6m)\omega\).

questions.stem: A uniform disk of mass \(M\) and radius \(R\) spinning at \(\omega_0\) about its vertical axis is set down flat on a horizontal surface with coefficient of kinetic friction \(\mu\). Its weight is spread evenly over its face. How long does it take to stop?
questions.explanation: A ring of radius \(r\) carries weight \(\dfrac{Mg}{\pi R^2}2\pi r\,dr\), so the friction torque is \(\displaystyle\int_0^R\mu\dfrac{2Mg}{R^2}r^2\,dr=\tfrac{2}{3}\mu MgR\). With \(I=\tfrac{1}{2}MR^2\), \(\alpha=\dfrac{4\mu g}{3R}\), and the time is \(\dfrac{\omega_0}{\alpha}\).

questions.stem: A wheel with rotational inertia \(3.0\text{ kg}\cdot\text{m}^2\), initially at rest, is acted on by a net torque \(\tau(t)=6t^2\), in newton-meters, from \(t=0\) to \(t=2.0\text{ s}\). What is its final angular speed?
questions.explanation: The angular impulse is \(\displaystyle\int_0^26t^2\,dt=16\text{ kg}\cdot\text{m}^2\text{/s}\), which equals the change in angular momentum. Dividing by \(I\) gives \(\dfrac{16}{3.0}\approx 5.3\text{ rad/s}\). Using the final torque, \(24\text{ N}\cdot\text{m}\), times the time gives too large a result.

questions.stem: A uniform solid cylinder, with rotational inertia \(\tfrac{1}{2}MR^2\), is placed on a rough horizontal surface sliding at speed \(v_0\) without rotating. What is its speed once it rolls without slipping?
questions.explanation: About a fixed point on the surface, friction exerts no torque, so \(Mv_0R=MvR+\tfrac{1}{2}MR^2\dfrac{v}{R}\), giving \(v=\tfrac{2}{3}v_0\). A solid sphere would keep \(\tfrac{5}{7}\) of its speed.

questions.stem: A satellite in a low circular orbit just above Earth's surface has a period of about 85 minutes. About what is the period of a satellite in a circular orbit of radius four times Earth's radius?
questions.explanation: For circular orbits around the same body, \(T\propto r^{3/2}\). Multiplying the radius by 4 multiplies the period by 8, to about 680 minutes. A geosynchronous orbit, with a 24-hour period, has a radius of about 6.6 Earth radii.

questions.stem: A child of mass \(m\) stands at the rim of a merry-go-round of radius \(R\) and rotational inertia \(I\), which turns freely at angular speed \(\omega_0\). The child walks to the center. What is the final angular speed?
questions.explanation: Angular momentum is conserved: \(\left(I+mR^2\right)\omega_0=I\omega\), since a child at the center contributes no rotational inertia. The child does work while walking inward, so the kinetic energy increases.

questions.skill: Work by static friction in rolling
questions.stem: A cylinder rolls without slipping down an incline. How much work does static friction do on it?
choices: A negative amount, because friction opposes the motion
None, because the point of contact is instantaneously at rest
A positive amount, because friction increases the cylinder's spin
A negative amount equal to the rotational kinetic energy gained
questions.explanation: Power delivered by a force is the force times the velocity of the material point where it acts, and the contact point of a rolling object has zero velocity. Friction converts some translational kinetic energy to rotational kinetic energy while doing no net work, so mechanical energy is conserved.

questions.stem: An object experiences an external force whose line of action passes through point P but not through point Q. About which point is the object's angular momentum conserved, if no other external forces act?
choices: About neither point, because a net force acts
questions.explanation: A force exerts no torque about any point on its line of action, so the angular momentum about P is unchanged. About Q the force has a lever arm, so the angular momentum about Q changes. Whether angular momentum is conserved depends on the reference point.

questions.stem: Two identical tops are tilted at the same angle, and top 1 spins twice as fast as top 2. How do their precession rates compare?
choices: Top 1 precesses twice as fast as top 2.
They precess at the same rate, because the torque of gravity is the same.
Top 1 precesses half as fast as top 2.
Top 1 precesses four times as fast as top 2.
questions.explanation: The precession rate is the torque divided by the spin angular momentum. The torque of gravity is the same for both, so the top with twice the angular momentum precesses at half the rate.

questions.stem: A planet moves in an elliptical orbit around a star. Which quantities are constant throughout the orbit?
choices: The planet's angular momentum about the star and the total mechanical energy of the planet–star system
The planet's speed and its kinetic energy
The planet's linear momentum and its distance from the star
The planet's kinetic energy and its angular momentum
questions.explanation: Gravity is a central, conservative force, so it exerts no torque about the star and does not change the total mechanical energy. The planet's speed, kinetic energy, and distance all vary around the orbit, and its momentum changes direction continuously.

questions.stem: A ball rolls without slipping across a rough floor and then onto a perfectly frictionless floor. What happens on the frictionless floor?
choices: It spins faster and slows down.
It stops, because no friction pushes it forward.
It keeps rolling with the same speed and the same rate of spin.
questions.explanation: On a level surface, rolling without slipping requires no friction once the speed and spin already match. With no horizontal force and no torque, both the velocity and the angular velocity stay constant.

questions.stem: A wheel rotates about a fixed axle through its center of mass. What is the wheel's total linear momentum?
choices: Zero, because its center of mass is at rest
\(MR\omega\), the mass times the rim speed
It cannot be determined without knowing the mass distribution
questions.explanation: The total momentum of any system equals its mass times the velocity of its center of mass. Each piece of the wheel is moving, but opposite pieces move in opposite directions, so their momenta cancel.

questions.stem: The position of an oscillator is \(x(t)=0.20\cos(5t)\), with \(x\) in meters and \(t\) in seconds. What is the magnitude of its maximum acceleration?
questions.explanation: Differentiating twice gives \(a=-(0.20)(5)^2\cos(5t)\), with maximum magnitude \(A\omega^2=0.20(25)=5.0\text{ m/s}^2\). The maximum speed is \(A\omega=1.0\text{ m/s}\).

questions.skill: Differential equation of simple harmonic motion
questions.stem: The motion of an object is described by \(\dfrac{d^2x}{dt^2}=-16x\), with \(x\) in meters and \(t\) in seconds. What is the period of the motion?
questions.explanation: Comparing with \(\dfrac{d^2x}{dt^2}=-\omega^2x\) gives \(\omega=4\text{ rad/s}\), so \(T=\dfrac{2\pi}{\omega}=\dfrac{\pi}{2}\text{ s}\).

questions.stem: A uniform rod of length \(L\), with rotational inertia \(\tfrac{1}{3}ML^2\) about its end, hangs from a pivot at one end and swings through small angles. What is its period?
questions.explanation: For a physical pendulum, \(T=2\pi\sqrt{\dfrac{I}{Mgd}}\), where \(d=\dfrac{L}{2}\) is the distance from the pivot to the center of mass. Then \(T=2\pi\sqrt{\dfrac{ML^2/3}{MgL/2}}=2\pi\sqrt{\dfrac{2L}{3g}}\).

questions.stem: A thin hoop of radius \(R\) hangs from a nail and swings through small angles in its own plane, as shown. The rotational inertia of a hoop about its center is \(MR^2\). What is the period of the oscillation?
questions.explanation: By the parallel-axis theorem the rotational inertia about the nail is \(MR^2+MR^2=2MR^2\), and the center of mass is a distance \(R\) from the pivot. \(T=2\pi\sqrt{\dfrac{2MR^2}{MgR}}=2\pi\sqrt{\dfrac{2R}{g}}\), the same as a simple pendulum of length \(2R\).

questions.stem: The graph shows the potential energy \(U(x)=x^3-6x^2+9x\), in joules, as a function of position \(x\), in meters, for a particle of mass \(1.5\text{ kg}\). What is the angular frequency of small oscillations about the stable equilibrium position?
questions.explanation: Near a minimum the potential energy is approximately \(\tfrac{1}{2}k_{\text{eff}}(x-x_0)^2\), with \(k_{\text{eff}}=\dfrac{d^2U}{dx^2}\). Here \(\dfrac{d^2U}{dx^2}=6x-12\), which is \(6\text{ N/m}\) at \(x_0=3\text{ m}\). Then \(\omega=\sqrt{\dfrac{6}{1.5}}=2\text{ rad/s}\).

questions.stem: A straight, frictionless tunnel is drilled through the center of a uniform, nonrotating planet of radius \(R\) whose surface gravitational field strength is \(g\). An object dropped into the tunnel oscillates. What is the period of its motion?
questions.explanation: Inside a uniform planet the gravitational force at distance \(r\) from the center is \(-\dfrac{mg}{R}r\), a linear restoring force with effective spring constant \(\dfrac{mg}{R}\). The period is \(2\pi\sqrt{\dfrac{m}{k}}=2\pi\sqrt{\dfrac{R}{g}}\), the same as the period of a satellite orbiting just above the surface.

questions.stem: Two blocks of mass \(m\) connected by a spring of spring constant \(k\) rest on a frictionless surface, as shown. The blocks are pulled apart and released from rest. What is the angular frequency of the oscillation?
questions.explanation: The center of the spring stays fixed, so each block oscillates on half of the spring, which has spring constant \(2k\). Then \(\omega=\sqrt{\dfrac{2k}{m}}\). Equivalently, the reduced mass of the pair is \(\dfrac{m}{2}\).

figure.alt: Position versus time graph of an oscillator: a cosine curve with amplitude 0.2 m and period 2 s, starting at x = 0.2 m when t = 0

questions.stem: The graph shows the position of an oscillator as a function of time. Which statement correctly relates the oscillator's velocity to its position?
choices: The velocity reaches its maximum one quarter of a period before the position does.
The velocity and the position reach their maxima at the same times.
The velocity reaches its maximum half a period after the position does.
The velocity is constant between the turning points.
questions.explanation: With \(x=A\cos\omega t\), the velocity is \(-A\omega\sin\omega t=A\omega\cos\!\left(\omega t+\tfrac{\pi}{2}\right)\), which leads the position by a quarter cycle. On the graph the position peaks at \(t=2\text{ s}\), and the slope is greatest at \(t=1.5\text{ s}\).

questions.stem: A block on a spring oscillates with amplitude \(A\). At what displacement from equilibrium is its kinetic energy equal to the potential energy stored in the spring?
questions.explanation: The energies are equal when the potential energy is half the total: \(\tfrac{1}{2}kx^2=\tfrac{1}{2}\left(\tfrac{1}{2}kA^2\right)\), so \(x=\dfrac{A}{\sqrt{2}}\). At \(x=\dfrac{A}{2}\) the potential energy is only one fourth of the total.

questions.stem: A block hung from a spring oscillates with period \(T\). The spring is cut in half, and the same block is hung from one of the halves. What is the new period?
questions.explanation: Half of a spring stretches half as far under the same force, so its spring constant is \(2k\). The period \(2\pi\sqrt{\dfrac{m}{k}}\) therefore decreases by a factor of \(\sqrt{2}\).

questions.stem: A simple pendulum of length \(L\) hangs from the ceiling of a car that has a constant horizontal acceleration \(a\). What is the period of small oscillations about its equilibrium position?
questions.explanation: In the car's frame the bob behaves as though gravity had magnitude \(\sqrt{g^2+a^2}\), tilted from the vertical by an angle with \(\tan\theta=\dfrac{a}{g}\). The pendulum oscillates about that tilted direction with the effective field strength in place of \(g\).

questions.stem: A block on a spring oscillates with angular frequency \(4\text{ rad/s}\). At \(t=0\) it is \(0.10\text{ m}\) from equilibrium and moving at \(0.40\text{ m/s}\). What is the amplitude of the oscillation?
questions.explanation: Energy conservation gives \(A^2=x_0^2+\dfrac{v_0^2}{\omega^2}=(0.10)^2+(0.10)^2\), so \(A=0.10\sqrt{2}\approx 0.14\text{ m}\). The block is not at its turning point at \(t=0\), because it is still moving.

questions.stem: A simple pendulum is released from rest at \(5^\circ\) from the vertical and its period is measured. It is then released from rest at \(60^\circ\). How does the second period compare with the first?
choices: It is the same, because the period of a pendulum does not depend on amplitude.
It is longer, because the restoring torque grows more slowly than the angular displacement at large angles.
It is shorter, because the bob moves faster.
It is shorter, because the restoring torque is larger.
questions.explanation: The restoring torque is proportional to \(\sin\theta\), which equals \(\theta\) only for small angles. At large angles \(\sin\theta<\theta\), so the restoring effect is weaker than simple harmonic motion requires and each swing takes longer. Independence of amplitude holds only in the small-angle limit.

questions.stem: A block on a spring oscillates on a frictionless horizontal surface with period \(T\). The same spring and block are then set oscillating on a frictionless incline, with the spring parallel to the incline. How do the period and the equilibrium position compare with the horizontal case?
choices: The period is longer, and the equilibrium position is shifted down the incline.
The period is shorter, and the equilibrium position is unchanged.
The period and the equilibrium position are both unchanged.
The period is the same, and the equilibrium position is shifted down the incline.
questions.explanation: The component of gravity along the incline is a constant force. It stretches the spring to a new equilibrium position but does not change how the net force varies with displacement from that position, which is still \(-kx\). The period remains \(2\pi\sqrt{\dfrac{m}{k}}\).

figure.alt: A block of mass m on a frictionless surface is attached to two springs, with spring constants k1 and k2, whose other ends are fixed to walls on either side

questions.stem: The two springs attached to the block shown are both stretched slightly at equilibrium because the walls are farther apart than the springs' combined natural lengths. How does this affect the period of oscillation?
choices: It shortens the period, because the springs are already under tension.
It lengthens the period, because the springs pull in opposite directions.
It has no effect, because the change in net force for a given displacement is still \(-(k_1+k_2)x\).
It prevents the block from oscillating.
questions.explanation: For ideal springs, the tension at equilibrium cancels and adds only a constant force to each side. The restoring force depends on how each spring's length changes from its equilibrium value, so the effective spring constant and the period are unchanged.

questions.stem: A uniform meter stick, with rotational inertia \(\tfrac{1}{12}ML^2\) about its center, is pivoted at its \(25\text{ cm}\) mark and swings through small angles. Using \(g=10\text{ m/s}^2\), what is its period?
questions.explanation: The pivot is \(0.25\text{ m}\) from the center of mass, so \(I=M\left(\tfrac{1}{12}+0.0625\right)\approx 0.146M\). Then \(T=2\pi\sqrt{\dfrac{I}{Mgd}}=2\pi\sqrt{\dfrac{0.146}{2.5}}\approx 1.5\text{ s}\). Treating the stick as a simple pendulum of length \(1\text{ m}\) gives \(2.0\text{ s}\).

questions.stem: A disk with rotational inertia \(0.020\text{ kg}\cdot\text{m}^2\) hangs from a wire whose torsion constant is \(0.50\text{ N}\cdot\text{m/rad}\), so that twisting it through angle \(\theta\) produces a restoring torque \(-\kappa\theta\). What is the period of its twisting oscillation?
questions.explanation: Newton's second law for rotation gives \(I\ddot\theta=-\kappa\theta\), the equation of simple harmonic motion with \(\omega=\sqrt{\dfrac{\kappa}{I}}=5.0\text{ rad/s}\). The period is \(\dfrac{2\pi}{5.0}\approx 1.3\text{ s}\).

questions.stem: A \(0.20\text{ kg}\) block hanging from a vertical spring oscillates with displacement \(y(t)=0.050\cos(10t)\), in meters, about its equilibrium position. Using \(g=10\text{ m/s}^2\), what is the greatest force the spring exerts on the block?
questions.explanation: From \(\omega^2=\dfrac{k}{m}\), \(k=20\text{ N/m}\). At equilibrium the spring is already stretched \(\dfrac{mg}{k}=0.10\text{ m}\), so its greatest stretch is \(0.15\text{ m}\) and its greatest force is \(20(0.15)=3.0\text{ N}\). The value \(1.0\text{ N}\) is only the additional force \(kA\).

questions.stem: A small uniform solid ball of radius \(r\), with rotational inertia \(\tfrac{2}{5}mr^2\), rolls without slipping back and forth near the bottom of a spherical bowl of radius \(R\). What is the period of small oscillations?
questions.explanation: The ball's center moves on a circle of radius \(R-r\). Because the ball's kinetic energy is \(\tfrac{7}{10}mv^2\) instead of \(\tfrac{1}{2}mv^2\), the effective inertia is \(\tfrac{7}{5}\) as large as for a sliding particle, so the period is longer by a factor of \(\sqrt{\tfrac{7}{5}}\).

questions.stem: An oscillator's position is \(x(t)=A\cos(\omega t+\phi)\). At \(t=0\) it is at \(x=0\) moving in the \(+x\) direction. What is \(\phi\)?
questions.explanation: \(x(0)=A\cos\phi=0\) requires \(\phi=\pm\dfrac{\pi}{2}\). The velocity \(v(0)=-A\omega\sin\phi\) is positive only if \(\sin\phi<0\), so \(\phi=-\dfrac{\pi}{2}\) and \(x=A\sin\omega t\).

questions.stem: A \(0.50\text{ kg}\) block on a spring of spring constant \(50\text{ N/m}\) is released from rest at \(x=A\). How long does it take to reach \(x=\dfrac{A}{2}\) for the first time?
questions.explanation: With \(\omega=\sqrt{\dfrac{50}{0.50}}=10\text{ rad/s}\), \(x=A\cos(10t)\) equals \(\dfrac{A}{2}\) when \(10t=\dfrac{\pi}{3}\), so \(t\approx 0.10\text{ s}\), one sixth of the period. Half the distance takes more than half the quarter-period, because the block starts from rest.

questions.stem: A block on a spring oscillates with amplitude \(A\). What fraction of its total mechanical energy is kinetic when it is a distance \(\dfrac{A}{3}\) from equilibrium?
questions.explanation: The spring energy at \(\dfrac{A}{3}\) is \(\tfrac{1}{2}k\dfrac{A^2}{9}\), one ninth of the total \(\tfrac{1}{2}kA^2\). The rest, eight ninths, is kinetic.

questions.stem: How does the acceleration of a simple harmonic oscillator compare with its position at every instant?
choices: It is in phase with the position.
It is exactly opposite in phase: proportional to the position and pointing the other way.
It leads the position by a quarter cycle.
It is constant, because the force is conservative.
questions.explanation: Differentiating \(x=A\cos\omega t\) twice gives \(a=-\omega^2x\). The acceleration reaches its positive maximum when the position reaches its negative maximum.

questions.stem: A block oscillates on a horizontal spring. At the instant it is at maximum displacement, a lump of clay is set gently on top of it and sticks. How do the amplitude and period change?
choices: The amplitude decreases and the period increases.
The amplitude is unchanged and the period increases.
The amplitude and period are both unchanged.
The amplitude increases and the period decreases.
questions.explanation: At maximum displacement the block is momentarily at rest, so adding the clay changes no momentum or energy, and the turning point stays the same. The greater mass lengthens the period, \(2\pi\sqrt{\dfrac{m}{k}}\).

questions.stem: Over one complete cycle of a spring–block oscillator, how does the time-averaged kinetic energy compare with the time-averaged spring potential energy?
choices: The average kinetic energy is greater.
The average potential energy is greater.
The average kinetic energy is zero, because the block returns to rest.
They are equal, each half of the total mechanical energy.
questions.explanation: Kinetic energy is proportional to \(\sin^2\omega t\) and potential energy to \(\cos^2\omega t\), and each averages to one half over a full cycle. Their sum is constant.

questions.stem: A particle moves under a restoring force \(F=-kx^3\) instead of \(F=-kx\). How does the period of its oscillation depend on its amplitude?
choices: The period decreases as the amplitude increases.
The period is independent of the amplitude.
The period increases as the amplitude increases.
questions.explanation: The force grows faster than linearly, so at larger amplitudes the particle is pushed back much harder and completes each cycle sooner; in fact the period is inversely proportional to the amplitude. Only a linear restoring force gives a period independent of amplitude.

questions.stem: Two identical spring–block oscillators are released from rest at the same instant, one displaced \(2\text{ cm}\) and the other \(6\text{ cm}\) from equilibrium. Which block reaches its equilibrium position first?
choices: The block released from \(2\text{ cm}\), because it has less distance to travel.
The block released from \(6\text{ cm}\), because it moves faster.
They reach it at the same time.
The block released from \(6\text{ cm}\), because the spring force on it is larger.
questions.explanation: In simple harmonic motion the period does not depend on amplitude, so both reach equilibrium a quarter period after release. The block with three times the distance to travel experiences three times the force and reaches three times the speed.
